#3757. Best Hunter Pets in WoW Forever

A Hunter isn't whole without their Pet, especially in WoW: Forever where Azeroth is a brave new frontier.

The Hunter’s Pet forms a core part of the Hunter experience in World of Warcraft: Forever, with much of their toolkit heavily relying on these partners in combat. In fact, the Hunter has become quite the iconic WoW Class for being able to tame a huge part of the MMO’s bestiary, giving players literally hundreds of options for Pets.

But for those still leveling their Hunters or curious for what other kinds of Pets are awaiting them all over Azeroth, there are indeed some creatures you should tame and fight with in specific situations.

When Forever launched on Nov. 4, Blizzard was quick to roll out a patch two days later (Nov. 6) to strengthen the ability of Hunter’s Pets to become semi-tanks, at least for the Hunters and smaller groups. But on Nov. 10, Blizzard rolled out a quick hotfix that streamlined some things about the Class:

We’re keeping track of how these changes can affect the performance of Pets so far, and we’ll update this list as necessary.

Hunters are DPS characters by nature, and a lot of that damage is usually facilitated by their Pets. And there are just some Pets that stand out among the rest as better damage dealers than their other counterparts. Cats are a standout here, as they’re among the most common Pet Families you can find as you level up.

Some iconic Cats you could aim for would be Broken Tooth (Badlands) and The Rake (Mulgore), but even the Mountain Lions in Hillsbrad can perform well if you’re not gunning for a rare find. Raptors are a close second among recommended damage Pets as they share the same damage mod as the Cat, whereas the Gorilla has a decent AOE and the Scorpid has a stacking Poison.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Hunter’s Pets don’t make good tanks, unlike traditional tanking Classes. With the right Pet Family, a Pet could still provide decent protection to your Hunter while you’re adventuring. Granted, they’re not as strong as we would want a “tanking” Pet to be, but these can take a beating and give a beating of their own.

Boars remain the best first Pets as they stun and give an attack boost to their next hit. If you level up Beast Mastery with the Boar, it might just be a long-term Pet. Meanwhile, Turtles and Crabs have the best defense stats among all Pets.

Say you want to tag along with a party but want to offer something other than having an extra member (your Pet) in tow. Then try to bring any one of these Pet Families in your dungeoning or leveling session. The idea here is that they’re not solely focused on dealing damage, but rather supporting the team in some capacity.

In this case, bring a Wolf to bolster everyone’s melee attack power. But if you feel you already have enough buffs, then a Carrion Bird to lower the enemy’s attack or a Tallstrider to lower the enemy’s armor could be more practical options.

Contrary to popular belief, the Hunter’s Pet should not focus on tanking in PvP, but rather on some form of control. The ideal PvP Pet should usually fit your current target at the moment, or if you’re unequipped to deal with a particular threat that you feel your Pet could help with.

Spiders usually win, as the 4-second rooting can be debilitating for most rotations and setups. If you prefer chasing down targets, then Hyenas and Crabs can slow them enough to leave them vulnerable.

There might be situations when you prefer to not really play with a Hunter’s Pet. Maybe you feel they’re just bringing you down, or you prefer the damage numbers when you’re performing solo.

You can perfectly go solo as a Marksmanship Hunter, courtesy of the Lone Wolf Talent. Getting this Talent gives you a 20% boost to all attacks as long as you don’t have an active Pet.

#3756. As investors ask about GTA 6 and AI, Take-Two CEO once again puts faith in dev creativity, states making hit games "remains the purview of human beings"

"Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future."

Today, as part of Take-Two Interactive Software's Q2 2027 earnings call, Strauss Zelnick fielded questions from investors after presenting the financial results of the company. One caller was concerned about AI - specifically about the proliferation of AI-powered compilations and decompilations that have been raising piracy concerns for publishers over the past few weeks.

Zelnick notes that "[the video games] business has been largely immune to piracy" thanks to factors like file size, how console ecosystems work, and aspects related to the online nature of the games industry. That said, Strauss continues, there is a threat posed to the industry because of AI. However, he assures listening investors that Take-Two is appropriately scaling its measures against bad faith actors using artificial intelligence.

"We are utterly focused on enhancing our technical defences and enhancing our legal activities appropriately. And - at the same time, without in any way being cavalier - every entertainment business that exists is subject to some element of piracy, [and] this is likely to invade our business to a greater or lesser extent. I think it will be manageable and we are focused on it."

Zelnick pivots back to AI again later in the call, where one investor once again asks about AI, seemingly keen to learn whether the CEO feels it can provide GTA 6 developer Rockstar with any kind of "competitive advantage" in the games industry. Given Zelnick's previous comments on the subject, his answer was not a complete surprise.

"It's always been true [that technology benefits us]," explains Zelnick. "We've always created our entertainment inside computers with technology. All advances have benefited us, and I don't expect that that will change - in fact, I hope it'll accelerate. I think at the same time, what we're known for [at Take-Two] is the desire to make the best entertainment on Earth. And, more often than not, we have succeeded - and the creativity that drives that success is human creativity harnessing technology. And I think that's what you'll see in the future, too.

"Undoubtedly some of the most recent technological advances that you've seen have made it easier to create assets. Where all that is consistent with the story of our business. When I started in interactive entertainment (longer ago than I would like to say), it was really difficult to create an asset in a computer. Today, it's a whole lot easier - but you know what's not easier? Making a big hit. Making a big hit was hard then, and it's hard now, and it's going to be hard in the future. And hit creation remains the purview of human beings."

This isn't the first instance of AI skepticism we've seen from Strauss Zelnick. Back in March, he outright rejected the idea that AI can tackle games on the scale of GTA 6. Elsewhere in the call, the Take-Two CEO reiterated how well GTA 6 is tracking as he reasserted pre-order numbers are well above expectations, and promised that the success of the game will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two's gaming business.

As someone who makes it a point to watch all the new streaming and made-for-TV holiday movies, including the entire Hallmark Countdown to Christmas lineup, I’m pretty used to plot holes, and they don't bother me much. However, after watching 12 Dates of Christmas, I can’t stop thinking about one confusing plot point: how come Christina’s (Lucy Hale) family didn’t recognize Peter (Ian Harding)?

The premiere of Hulu's 12 Dates of Christmas on the 2026 TV Schedule serves as a mini reunion for Pretty Little Liars fans, as it reunites Hale and Harding for the holiday flick. Hale plays Christina, a workaholic who owns a furniture restoration shop and has made little time for finding her romantic soulmate. After a disastrous family Christmas Eve dinner, Christina makes a promise to herself and her mom that by next year she’ll have someone to bring to it. Of course, the year gets away from her, which leads her best friend (Kahyun Kim) to set up a string of dates for Christina to go on in the twelve weeks leading up to Christmas Eve.

In the midst of the endless stream of disastrous dates, Christina reconnects with her high school crush Peter (Harding), who commissions Christina to refurbish a beloved loveseat for the home he’s remodeling with the help of local mean girl Bridget (Greer Grammer). The two regularly cross paths, and Peter even meets Christina’s entire family when he drives her to the hospital after learning her sister is in labor.

It’s no surprise that Hale and Harding have amazing chemistry and make it easy to root for their characters to get their happily ever after despite the obstacles between them. However, after the infamous hospital scene, I felt myself growing more and more confused as to why Chrsitina’s family seemed to not know who Peter was, considering Christina had a crush on him in high school.

Netflix’s A Dog’s Perfect Christmas Made Me Cry, But Not For The Reasons I Thought

Sure, not every daughter shares their high school crush with their family, but Christina’s family is the meddling type, especially her mom. It doesn’t make sense that they wouldn’t at least know about Peter from her high school pining days. I can maybe believe that they wouldn’t recognize him because he’s older now, but not even getting excited at the name just doesn’t make any sense.

Not to mention, this is a Christmas romance movie, which means the town Christina grew up in and still calls home isn’t a big one. All the more reason for her family to at least recognize Peter’s name, especially since he’s renovating his family’s home.

Ultimately, Christina’s family not knowing who Peter is isn’t that big of a deal. However, I do think it would have been a fun twist if they did recognize him because it would make them meddle in her love life even more. Still, 12 Dates of Christmas is a cute and festive Christmas flick that anyone with a Hulu subscription should definitely check out.

#3754. Spider-Man 2 And A Bunch Of Other Great Games Are About To Look Even Better On Base PS5

Spider-Man 2‘s dazzling cityscapes are about to be even more breathtaking. It’s one of several games that are adding support for Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR), Sony’s new AI upscaling tech for improving resolution on base PS5.

It’s essentially a weaker version of the PSSR upscaling used on PS5 Pro to boost image quality even at higher framerates. Ghost of Yotei and Marvel’s Wolverine were the first games to support QSSR when it was revealed back in early October. Now the following games have been added to the list and will be rolling out support throughout the rest of 2026:

Remedy Entertainment graphics programmer Erik Jansson said QSSR creates a more stable and detailed image. “We can deliver increased sharpness, better environmental clarity and overall visual improvements to even more PlayStation players,” said Embark Studios technical director Mikael Linderholm.

Some players might hurt themselves squinting to see the differences, even in side-by-side comparisons, but it’s still cool to see the six-year-old PS5 being able to deliver improved graphics without any actual hardware changes. QSSR grew out of Sony’s collaboration with AMD called Project Amethyst. Hopefully it leads to more post-processing improvements in the future, and ones that more games are able to take advantage of without too much extra work.

#3753. How to raid other players in ROB RUN

ROB RUN has many ways for you to expand your criminal empire, and raiding other players is certainly a good strategy. While the method isn’t as easy as breaking into NPC houses, you can master the art by following some simple tips.

First, you need to obtain Breach Decoders.

The first task is to get the Decoders, and there are different ways to get them. Uncommon Decoders are the easiest ones to get, and you can obtain them from cabinets, safes, and different containers. You can also find some from the Season 1 battle pass.

If you want to have the Epic Decoder, you can obtain it by exchanging the Uncommon variant. Go to Lenny’s Motel, and you’ll find a barter trader who will provide you with the item for $10,000.

When you’re about to raid a player base, you’ll need to have multiple Decoders. Unlike a house, a player base is a lot more complex when it comes to completing a breach. Each part requires a separate Decoder (or more than one) to gain entry.

In simple words, you’ll need to bring a Decoder for every base part that has a security system.

Completing a raid is pretty simple as long as you have the required Decoders. You have to use them to strip away points from a security terminal until it hits zero. The number of points you have to strip varies across different parts.

While the Fuse slots for a part don’t change, its tier will determine the number of Decoders you’ll need to open them.

#3752. Switch 2 and Switch consoles updated to version 23.5.0 as Nintendo quietly re-introduces eShop gifting

Nintendo has just pushed out a new update to all Switch and Switch 2 consoles, bringing the firmware on both up to version 23.5.0. The headline change with the new update is support and compatibility for an upcoming update that will allow members of a Nintendo Account family group to gift games to one another.

The feature itself is expected to go live on 17th November, 2026. "Just in time for the holidays, a new feature will let family group members gift digital games to other members of their group," says a post on a dedicated blog on the Nintendo site. "You will be able to gift digital products that you purchase through Nintendo eShop on your device to family group members. This includes eligible games as well as DLC and upgrade packs. As a reminder, anyone with a Nintendo Account can easily set up a family group and add members (up to 8 total)."

The publisher notes, however, that "some products may not be eligible for digital gifting" and that "supervised accounts are not able to send digital gifts". Additionally, "the number of digital gift purchases allowed in a given period is limited".

"This feature is a great way to celebrate a special occasion with your kids. Happy gifting!" concludes Nintendo. Just in time for the holidays, how thoughtful. It's worth noting that a previous iteration of this support was included back on the Nintendo Wii, but that was much more robust than this - back then, the publisher allowed users to send WiiWare or Virtual Console games to anyone on their Wii Friend list via the Wii Shop Channel, rather than just those limited to their immediate group. This functionality was lost in 2019, alongside the closure of the Wii Shop Channel.

Storm's reworked legendary skin will be here for Christmas.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Skin distribution seems to be an issue in pretty much any game with more than one hero and clear favourites. Marvel Rivals has come under fire for it for a while now, ever since players got wise to which heroes were favourites and which had clearly been shoved to the side.

It all came to a head a few months ago when the summer skins were released, and it was revealed that Storm was the only female hero to not get a legendary costume among all the swimsuit designs. Players did not look upon this favourably, as Storm is a hugely popular character and had already gone a long time without the same kind of legendary skins as other heroes like Luna Snow and had been passed over for skins in the Disco and Egyptian God skin lines.

But all the player complaints seem to have gotten through to NetEase, with creative director Guangyun Chen acknowledging in a dev diary that "season 10 has been a challenging one for us." Not only were players upset about only one hero being released this season, but the devs have "been closely following the community's feedback regarding certain heroes receiving fewer costumes. With strong demands for more high-quality Legendary costumes featuring recolours and ultimate ability visual upgrades."

The decision has since been made to upgrade Storm's summer skin to legendary tier with the devs "targeting a release around Christmas this December" for it. Other slightly forgotten heroes who will be getting some visual upgrades include Human Torch, who will get a legendary costume in early December which includes "recolours and ultimate ability VFX". Cloak and Dagger will also be getting a (presumably Valentines Day-themed) skin in February.

"We've been hard at work at this for almost eight months," Guangyun Chen says. "Cloak's design will include full legs. We fully re-animated Cloak's entire movement set strictly for this, we really hope you enjoy it."

But with all these new redesigns and costumes on the way, Guangyun Chen wants to remind players that skins can't just be made or changed at a moment's notice: "Please understand that art asset production requires a certain lead time and simply can't be done overnight. Generally, a single costume takes eight to 10 months to produce from start to finish."

Storm's redesigned summer skin has been in the works for three months already, with the finished product coming out after five months of work. That's under the average of eight to 10 months, but this sounds like the exception not the rule.

#3750. Devs Promise To Pay $5,000 To Help Cover Your Divorce If You Can Be The First To Beat Their Lock-Picking Game

In this oversaturated climate, I’m never gonna be mad at a developer’s unique attempt to get people to play their gameâwithin reason of courseâand this is one of those times. The developers at Collision Games are offering $5,000 USD toward the divorce (or wedding!) of the first person who can beat their love lock-picking game, Love Locks.Â

The rules are simple. Register your email and SteamID; then, when the game launches on December 3rd, be the fastest to unlock 100,000 love locks that have been plastered across a bridge in Paris, making this perfect for speedrunners looking to make a…quick buck. Players will have all kinds of tools at their disposal including bolt cutters and a drone they can use to go magnet-fishing for keys in the River Seine. The competition ends on December 10th, giving players roughly seven days to chew through all 100,000 of the game’s love locks.

Once the competition period ends, the devs will announce the winner, and they’ll have two years to send Collision Games a bill for an eligible wedding or divorce expense like buying a pretty dress or hiring an expensive lawyer (no, really). If the winner is already happily married or divorced, they can nominate a family member or friend to receive the prize. There are specific age and country-of-origin eligibility requirements for entry so check out the full list of rules and requirements here.

I never really got love locks as a concept. You and your sweetheart want to demonstrate the durability of your love by defacing public property with an easily circumventable pad lock? An action that is widely considered to be a public nuisance, if not ecologically harmful? Makes sense then for someone to make a game about getting rid of all those eyesores, love be damned.

#3749. Xbox CEO celebrates company’s 25 years on social media but can’t stop herself from hinting at further downsizing and AI usage

"A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations."

Happy birthday, Xbox! Here’s to 25 years of human-made entertainment, and 25 more with way fewer developers and way more generative AI.

That’s what CEO Asha Sharma seems to be insinuating with her words today in a reflection on 25 years of Xbox, of which she has been a part for less than one. And yet, her impact has been tremendous, with a massive overhaul this year in her “reset” involving the layoffs of thousands of workers to get the business profitable again.

And it sounds like even more layoffs are to come. We already know that, but the number could be bigger, judging by the tone of her social media post where she champions new technology that we haven’t even begun to feel the full effects of.

“Throughout human history, the scale of what we could create was determined by the people, capital, and resources we could command,” Sharma said. “That relationship is beginning to break. A single person will soon be able to wield capabilities that once required entire nations. A small team will be able to build worlds that today demand hundreds of developers and hundreds of millions of dollars.”

How else would a “a single person” or “a small team” build games that normally take hundreds of people besides cutting costs and using generative AI technology in the stead of those who made games before? And where will those hundreds of people go when they are no longer needed? To the unemployment line, of course!

“While modern games demonstrate the heights of human craft in ways unimaginable just decades ago, the cost, resources, and risk required to create them have grown just as dramatically,” she said. “As a result, too many ideas never become games, and too many games fall short of what their creators imagined. For decades, this has been the unavoidable tradeoff of ambition. We must change this.”

Sharma said she believes “the future of gaming will look more like its beginning, when a small team with a big idea could change how the world plays.” Take from all of this what you will, but what I’m taking from it is she’s saying, in many words, “we will be using AI tools and replacing people with them, so get used to it.” React accordingly.

The Ocarina of Time launch also caused US hardware spending to jump by 81 percent during the week ending 31st October compared to the same period last year.

#3747. Under pressure, Big Walk studio reveals it used generative AI "sparingly" while making its hit 2026 game

"It has become a matter of public interest."

Australian developer House House has revealed it used generative AI "sparingly" to help make celebrated, indie, multiplayer puzzle game Big Walk.

In a statement sent to Aftermath - following a judging fallout related to the Independent Games Festival - House House revealed it had used large language models primarily to help debug the game's code.

"In the final stretch of Big Walk's development, LLMs were used sparingly by House House to help work through difficult technical challenges and bugs," the developer said. "In some cases, snippets from LLM responses were copied as a starting point to be modified into game code - we'd estimate that well under 0.1 percent of Big Walk's code had anything to do with this usage, and generative AI was not used in any other context when making the game."

House House added: "The primary use case for House House's use of LLMs was to research, via chatbots, issues we encountered with third-party code."

The studio's revelation comes after a sizeable number of IGF jurors - 19 of them - issued a statement saying they would not vote for any game that used generative AI during its development. This was done after seeing "a significant increase" in entry submissions involving generative AI use, which "set off some fairly intense discussion and disagreement across the judge and jury pools". And rather than not vote for these in silence, a collection of jurors decided to take a public stand.

House House hadn't disclosed Big Walk generative AI use anywhere before disclosing it for its IGF submission. "We have not made any disclosure on Steam as the platform does not request disclosure of code or chatbot usage," the studio explained. "We are posting this disclosure as it has become a matter of public interest."

House House added: "This is not an endorsement of, or argument for, the use of AI tools, however minimal. We have some concern that voluntary disclosures like this might contribute to the normalisation of this technology, or its treatment as 'inevitable'. We support the work of those who are trying to limit the harm generative AI is doing to video games and our world, and apologise that Big Walk's LLM usage may not meet their standards.

"Big Walk was developed without an internal AI usage policy in place, and we consider that lack of policy a failure. We will work to have a more comprehensive policy going forwards."

It's a revelation that's likely to leave a taint of some degree on one of this year's brightest stars - a game Eurogamer awarded a full five stars to in its Big Walk review.

#3746. 60 FPS Zelda or 30 FPS GTA 6, that is the question

30 FPS in 2026, Absolute Cinema or actual Grand Theft?

GTA 6 will be targeting 30 FPS on consoles, per the crucial intel that Rockstar only released far into the most successful preorder campaign ever. Nintendo, on the other hand, stole everyone’s hearts with Ocarina of Time’s 60 FPS version. Will this impact how we see GTA 6?

Rockstar was already $1 billion deep in preorder gold when it revealed that GTA 6 would run at the same framerate that GTA 5 ran at back in 2012. In truth, that was expected, because if it was going to run at 60 FPS, the studio certainly would’ve mentioned it at some point, but this is the kind of news that will always disappoint people who aren’t constantly looking for GTA updates. How much of a dealbreaker could this be? The answer is complex.

I think a good example is that of Bloodborne, a game that barely keeps 30 FPS for one second, but it’s still one of my favorite games of all time. Why? Because it’s that good, and because it was made under the assumption that the team likely wouldn’t get it to run at 60 frames per second on PS4 hardware.

As for GTA 5, most people would’ve preferred it to run at 60 fps even back then, but fans just knew the game would be pushing the PS3 and Xbox 360’s hardware—yes, GTA 5 originally released on those systems—to the limit, so everyone just felt very glad they were even getting something that looked so amazing. Also, GTA 5 pulled off some nice frame pacing, which means that the game didn’t often dip below the targeted mark, and its stability almost made it feel like it was running at a higher framerate than it actually was.

I think players will end up accepting GTA 6’s framerate, because even though a higher count has become much more common these days, GTA 6 is likely going to achieve a solid 30 FPS, which is very different from “targeting” it.

But there’s a possible obstacle on Rockstar’s path: the recently released Ocarina of Time Remake. It runs at a beautifully nimble 60 FPS and is selling so well that there surely will be a lot of overlap between player bases, and that might very well start the 30 vs 60 debate again.

Sure, the games have very different gameplay styles and scope. Still, many gamers need to turn everything into a competition, and Zelda is running on considerably weaker hardware. Nintendo could’ve probably gotten away with Ocarina of Time running at 30 frames per second, because the original ran at under 20. To get Ocarina of Time to run any worse than that, you’ll need the hacked Sega 32X port.

We would always eat up all that sweet Ocarina music regardless of the speed Nintendo played it at, but the company still found us deserving of that extra silky-smooth experience. With all that, those who are all about smooth over cinematic will inevitably question why Rockstar didn’t tone down the graphical fidelity a bit to give us more fluid gameplay for consoles that cost upwards of $800.

And while I can’t tell you exactly why Rockstar made that choice, I remember that running at 60fps was the biggest selling point for GTA 5‘s PC port, so Rockstar might just be going for a tried-and-true sales strategy. Either way, I believe most people will truly enjoy GTA 6 as it comes out, but I’m 100% sure people will only go absolutely nuts for it once it reaches the PC and its sky-high framerate ceilings.

GTA 6 will come out on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X|S on November 19, and might release on PC earlier than you expect.

The Gen-Z comedy, Adults, dropped its sophomore season on FX and Hulu as part of the 2026 TV Schedule back in August, and since then fans have been loudly campaigning for another season. After months of waiting, the series was officially renewed for a Season 3, much to the delight of the fans.

The cast took to Instagram to share the news with their devoted viewers, which included the reveal that the third season will include 16 original episodes, nearly double the length of the first two seasons. As a massive fan of the show and a firm believer that sitcoms need more episodes, I’m thrilled at the news! In fact, I’m so excited I’ve already compiled a list of things I absolutely need the extended season to feature.

Holiday episodes used to be a sitcom staple, but as television seasons started getting shorter and shorter, these episodes started to disappear. I had accepted the fact that I would never get to see my favorite characters celebrate birthdays or the holiday season, but now that might not be the case.

With a 16-episode season comes space for these beloved one-off episodes. Just think of all the hijinks that could ensue from the Adults gang trying to celebrate the holidays. We’ve already seen them struggle to host a sophisticated dinner party in the first season. Now imagine it’s the holiday season and Paul Baker’s family decides to make the trek to New York to spend Christmas with their son and his new husband after his sister lets it slip that he’s married. The shenanigans would be hilarious!

Over the course of the first two seasons, Adults has found time to include some fun guest stars like actor Charlie Cox, actress/model Julia Fox, and sitcom royalty Raven-Symoné. I’m sure the tradition will continue in Season 3, and I have some ideas on whom the creators should reach out to.

Since Adults films in Canada, it makes total sense that the Gen-Z show should approach a breakout Gen-Z actor who also appears on a hit Canadian-produced show. Yes, I’m talking about Heated Rivalry’s Hudson Williams. Williams could play himself and act as an old friend from Paul Baker’s childhood, since he canonically grew up in Canada and has a history of befriending famous people without realizing it.

Another obvious, albeit more difficult to get, choice would be New York’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani. I can totally see Issa finding a way to reach out to the Mayor about some minor inconvenience affecting her city that no one else cares about.

Season 2 ended on a major high note with Paul Baker and Anton finally getting together, but it also shocked fans with a plot twist in the final moments that featured Billie and Samir hooking up. Don’t get me wrong, I can’t wait to see Paul Baker and Anton enter their “relationship era,” but I’m also excited to see what shenanigans Billie and Samir get into now that they’ve crossed such a huge line in their friendship.

On one hand, I’d love Billie and Samir to channel the relationship between Chandler and Monica from Friends and try to keep their hookup and subsequent relationship a secret from the rest of the house. It would be difficult considering how close they all are, but definitely worth it to keep it away from everyone meddling.

However, I could also see them trying to act as if their hookup was casual and something they can continue doing without catching feelings. Neither Billie nor Samir do anything without their whole heart involved, so this would be a recipe for disaster but also great for laughs.

Season 3 has so much room for fun and hijinks with its longer episode order, and I can’t wait to see what the writers come up with. While it’ll be a while before the new season is out, fans can stream the first two seasons with a Hulu subscription now.

#3742. All Treasure Rooms in Queen’s Domain and how to find them

Queen’s Domain has five Treasure Rooms, and locating them can be a difficult task. These secret areas are challenging to find, but they offer valuable rewards. In this guide, I will make things easy for you to find all five of them.

Before we can venture to find the treasure vaults, the first task is to get the Keystones. You will need them to open the vaults. Once you reach Obmuer Temple, you can find the first Keystone.

Make your way through the water until you reach a point where a broken structure slopes upwards. Go past it and use the edge to air dash to move forward. You’ll come across a small plot of land where you find one of Aganmi’s missing raiders.

From there, you’ll find an opening in the temple to your right. Drop, and then turn left to find the dark cave. Continue straight, and you’ll find a ledge that drops into a large room with pillars. Go to the other side of the room, enter the open vault, and you’ll find a skeleton sitting with a note next to it.

Read this note to get the Blood Keystone from the shop for 24 Ancient Coins.

There are two Blood Treasure Rooms, and you can find the first one in the basement of the Tower of Knowledge. Once you defeat the boss, clear the growths. This allows you to access a room filled with candle crawlers.

Clear out the enemies, and you’ll discover the door to the Blood Vault. Inside, you’ll get the Rusted Greatsword.

To find the next Blood Vault, head to Verdant Hollow. Go through the Petrified Garden and walk out of the gate that connects the Rotting Cavern and Verdant Hollow.

You can do so using the elevator from the Verdant Hollow wing altar. Walk into the cave from the ledge, and you’ll find the dark room.

Head to Neasied to find the first Velvet Treasure Room. You will find a cave on one side of the area that has the altar on the cliff face. Enter the cave and go all the way down to find a hole. This hole will lead you to another room. Follow the path, and you will eventually reach the elevator that takes you all the way down. You will find the treasure room entrance at this location.

To find the next one, head to the Rotting Cavern. Look for a shine-like structure and follow the path that leads you to it. Eventually, you will come across a sealed door that requires four dark triangular slit pieces. You can find these pieces around the area, and I believe their locations are random. Once you find them, they will lead you to the vault.

There is only one Jade Treasure Room, and you will find it in the Deimpo Mausoleum. Go to the wing altar and take the door on the right. This will lead you to a giant stairwell, and as you descend, you will find the door to the vault.

"If you want to make a videogame like Grand Theft Auto, you need animators, you need musicians, you need so many people from across the creative industries to make them work. And why shouldn't it be our children in our communities who get the chance to get those jobs?"

It's fascinating how things change. I. for instance, used to love staying up all night playing videogames; now I get mad at the world if I miss my bedtime by 10 minutes. In kind of a similar vein, Grand Theft Auto was once the poster child for everything insidious, dangerous, and downright wrong about videogames, but now we have a member of the UK government—a secretary of state, no less—talking about how the upcoming Grand Theft Auto 6 is something the whole country should be proud of.

"My love for videogames knows no bounds, and I am an avid addict of things like Animal Crossing and the Mario series," Lisa Nandy, the UK's secretary of state for digital, culture, media, and sport, told The Rundown. "I'm not sure I get away with taking a day off to do it, but I think it's something that we can be really proud of.

"One of the reasons that we're investing in arts and music and all of those things that give people the chance to live richer, larger lives is because we are creating jobs in these incredible industries. And if you want to make a videogame like Grand Theft Auto, you need animators, you need musicians, you need so many people from across the creative industries to make them work. And why shouldn't it be our children in our communities who get the chance to get those jobs?"

I'm as politically cynical as most folks, and sure, Nandy is using the moment opportunistically to promote her government—although, cynicism notwithstanding, I do respect her ability to stay on-message by turning a softball question about GTA 6 into talking about job creation.

At the same time, though, this is a remarkable turnaround from, say, 20 years ago, when everyone in a position of authority lost their minds over the Hot Coffee mod for GTA: San Andreas. Some of you might not be old enough to remember (you have no idea how much it pains me to say that) but referring to GTA as a legitimate cultural export in the early 2000s would've got any mainstream Western politician laughed out of the room—and suggesting that it'd be cool if the children (the children!) grew up to make more games like that? Pure political suicide.

As PC Gamer's Evan Lahti wrote in 2017, "Any American who played games in the '90s remembers the period of pearl-clutching and pseudoscientific fear-mongering from senators like Joe Lieberman, who led a call to ban violent videogames." This was serious stuff back then, and it wasn't really until the US Supreme Court ruled that videogames, like other creative works, are protected speech under the First Amendment that the hysteria and hand-wringing started to meaningfully die down.

But now here we are, 15 years later: The Miami Heat are cosplaying as a Vice City sports team, Rockstar is holding a huge GTA music festival featuring Cardi B and Travis Scott, half the state of Florida is embracing a Leonida transformation (and the cops aren't even mad about it), and now we've got the UK government saying it's all quite grand—splendid, even. Time, man. It really is a river carving the bedrock of our souls.

#3740. Phantom Blade Zero: The Kotaku Review

As I launched Phantom Blade Zero for the first time and began what I can only describe as a belabored compiling of shaders, I used the time to dig out a notebook buried at the bottom of a moving box containing notes I took during a preview of the game in 2024. At the time, I was tapped by another outlet to take the Summer Game Fest preview because everyone on staff was busy. No one was expecting this action game with flashy trailers and an overly wordy title would be all that worth paying attention to, so it was handed to me to see what it was all about.Â

Two years later, sitting down to play the final game, I kept flashing back to that demo with developer S-Game, who were so desperate to get media attention on their title in the very first appointment of the very first day. They were so worried every time I died, asking me if I needed to turn down the difficulty, deathly afraid I was going to saunter over to the media room and lambast the game for my many deaths during a half-hour demo. And some part of me wonders, playing the final game, is past-me the reason for the annoyances current-me has with an otherwise incredible action game?

âIâve got Soul but Iâm not a soldier.â

The feel is incredible, combat is intense, the game is content-packed, some of the boss fights are among the best Iâve ever seen.

Way too easy to miss quests and items, some gimmick bosses just donât work, Iâm conflicted on the way standard enemy encounter design functions, story is frustratingly told.

65 hours. Despite missing a few quests, finished every side quest and got the True Ending. Thereâs a âsecond cycleâ plus game for the real sickos.

Phantom Blade Zero is an action game that is more 3D Ninja Gaiden than Soulslike, though it absorbs and molds some Soulslike traditions and mechanics to varying degrees of success. As a multitude of combat scenarios, Phantom Blade is an unqualified success. The core act of pressing buttons to attack, parry, and dodge feels immaculately wonderful, especially given that the premise demands you do all those things at once. Where Phantom Blade differs from, say, a Sekiro or Onimusha: Way of the Sword is in the way it expectsânay, demandsâthat you throw the traditional notion of balancing attack and defense out the window. Phantom Blade will occasionally present enemies that attack you utterly relentlessly, with literally only frames of breathing room between flurries.

The solution is not one of timing, but of boldness. The game isnât trying to force you to find the right opportunity; it wants you to keep parrying or keep the block button held down and also attack or dodge as the situation demands. Trusting that protagonist Soul can handle this is the first major difficulty spike to overcome, because it does not feel at all like something you should be able to do, and morphs into the only way you can perceive playing action games by the end of your journey.

You might be tempted to take that as an exaggeration, but I insist that itâs not. Once Phantom Blade Zeroâs everything-all-at-once combat clicked for me, it genuinely felt like I was going to have trouble going back to melee systems that do not require beckoning the icy touch of arthritis at a young age. It is not particularly deepâyou pretty much learn to tap the parry button with a constant rhythm and time the bigger hits for combat advantages and dopamine releaseâbut it feels exciting and active. If Phantom Blade ZeroÂ was only going to nail one thing, itâs an overwhelmingly good thing the game nailed this.

One thing that Phantom Blade ZeroÂ does not nail, however, is the story. The narrative has the unfortunate combination of being both overbearing and incomprehensible for much of its dozens of hours, throwing a tome of unexplained proper nouns at you so large that it would make Final Fantasy XIIIâs opening hours blush.

The genre is no stranger to bad or underexplained stories; it might even be argued that the disposable narratives are part and parcel of excellent character action. But Phantom Blade Zero is not that. It does not treat its narrative or worldbuilding as something that most players will discard and ignore. For whatever reason, S-Game has decided that the story in this title must be omnipresent and decidedly interruptive, littering the game with cutscenes, lore scrolls, collectibles of magic audio logs, and pages and pages of descriptions of weapons and enemies.

I do not wish to turn my nose up at this out of hand. A strong story can and should enhance a game, but I cannot overemphasize how spitefully Phantom Blade tells its story in its early hours. It is borderline frustrating how little the game tells you of what any of the names and terms the dialogue is constantly throwing around actually mean. It was dozens of hours before I grasped what was going on in the story, a timeframe not aided by the fact that its writers insist on forcing it to unfold like a mystery. Poring over the logs of enemies to understand who it was I was just fighting and what relationship they had to the act of Transcension, or the organization of the Order, or maybe itâs the Mandate, or perhaps he was with the Thread-Binding Sect, or the Baishan Sect, or maybe Iâm just going to go take a nap because this is too much, it all ended up just making me feel like I came into a movie midway through and everyone is having a good time but me.

When I did eventually wrap my mind around the ongoing plot, I enjoyed learning about the various ways the world had essentially ended, though it took me a long time to understand if it had happened a hundred years ago, or one year ago, or was currently happening, and it was not worth the miles the game dragged my captive and ignorant ass across to get there.

That the gameâs story has a climax that breaks down major revelations in a 20-minute Chinese Opera performed with shadow puppets leaves me scratching my head over whether I should be applauding the ambition or tut-tutting the sledgehammer taken to the pacing, but either way I was not having a good time.

The story may be burdensome, but it is not what Iâm thinking about when fighting the gameâs copious amount of bosses. Soul steps into a new boss fight every few feet, often for spurious narrative reasons, and the quality of these fights varies wildly, with some extreme high points and some unfortunate low points. There are boss fights that I can truthfully say are among the best Iâve seen in an action game, both in terms of gameplay and aesthetics. One such example is the consummate rival fight, where Soul defends himself against his former student and her two bodyguards. The battle is a pitch-perfect realization of proper escalation, with you fighting the boss in a clash of swords, then tackling a second phase in which she transforms into a pugilist with fists of iron, and finally taking on all three enemies at once while the sun sets in the background and the slow piano music adds more instruments and intensity.

There are some gimmick fights that try to play with the mechanics and force you to act in different ways that mostly donât work. One fight tries to punish you for parrying, another only lets you damage the enemy after parrying certain attacks, and the novelty of these battles wears off when youâre midway through their large HP bars and realize you still have half a fight left to go. Thankfully, the good boss encounters greatly outnumber these, but they do make you feel a bit like you just slammed face-first into a tunnel painted onto the side of a wall.

One boss fight has Soul taking on a troupe of Lion Dancers who spit fire and, midway through the encounter, the head Lion Dancer dances on some poles across the arena while he and Soul fling fireballs at each other as Soul gets up on his own set of dancing poles. Itâs a really smart way to break up the boss fight, but I also feel like it would not have needed to break up the boss fight if it werenât so long and the effort to chip away HP so arduous.

Structurally, Phantom Blade has Soul running through various environments with numerous branching paths at every turn and a smattering of enemies along the way. These enemies arenât meant to be overly difficult and nothing bears that out more obviously than the fact that, when one is defeated, they stay defeated. This means that combat with minor enemies is never an insurmountable obstacle; definitionally, it cannot be. Encounters are not puzzles for you to solve; you just throw Soul at them, defeating one member of the group and then having an easier time the next time you arrive at full health. Considering thereâs no punishment for death, this design choice feels like it boils the game down to an exploratory boss rush with some enemies hanging around between them, just to keep you pressing buttons.

Thatâs not to say youâll never have a problem with a standard enemy, but that ultimately those problems do not really matter. Given enough time, enemies are merely rocks being shaped by erosion, and you are the wind sending waves to crash against them. Maybe that makes the game easier for some, but itâs a design decision that inherently feels like it robs you of stakes that would have otherwise been interesting.

Iâve gone back and forth on whether the permanently despawned enemies make for a good idea or not. On one hand, it does make much of the encounter design feel like a conveyer belt with no sense that I was overcoming obstacles. But flipping a switch to change that one thing would not work with the rest of the game as itâs currently designed. It would be beyond wearisome to have to search for the gameâs optional areas and collectibles while fighting through the respawning enemies. Phantom Blade doesnât have many Soulslike runbacks to bosses, but those that exist would become significantly more aggravating if you had to burn a heal on the way thanks to an overly aggressive enemy swiping at you from offscreen.

Toward the end of the game, this does change, though perhaps the pendulum swings a little too far the other way as enemies with tediously large health pools and hyperaggressive attack patterns become significantly more common. While I would have liked a more considered sense of balance in the encounter design throughout, I prefer the back half, where the game offers a bit more bite, to its early sections which hand-wave you through.

The number of optional paths in the game is truly worthy of awe. Within the first half hour, youâre given a side quest that wonât t resolve until near the end of the game, you may encounter an optional boss thatâll slice Soul in half in a single hit with verbal warnings to come back later, and you can pick up another side quest to find a flower for a girl that ends up taking you multiple chapters to fully suss out. No one can accuse Phantom Blade Zero of not playing the long game, and I think that aspect on its own both feels cool and aids in making the quests feel like part of a journey.

But as with many things this game does, it sometimes feels like the cool aspects are simply giving S-Game permission to do something extremely annoying on the other side of them. In the case of side quests, Phantom Blade revels in having missable objectives that can end up fully locking you out of things you might have wanted to see, up to and including the self-titled True Ending. It doesnât take much to miss a quest, either through progressing a little too far without reaching a satisfactory movement point in the questline, answering with the wrong dialogue choices, defeating a boss you werenât supposed to, or in one case, not talking to NPCs before picking up an item.

Sometimes you get a warning about this happening and maybe only have yourself to blame, but many times you do not. In a breezy action game that youâll be running through multiple times, I can get the desire to cheekily tell the player, too bad, try again on the next cycle! But motherfucker, this game is at least 50 hours long on a casual initial playthrough. If I miss a side quest, I am done. It might as well not exist at that point. This is the kind of game where youâll have to consult a guide at the beginning of every chapter and follow it thoroughly if you want to see everything, or just make peace with the fact that you just wonât see it all.

One aspect of Phantom Blade that deserves calling out is the gameâs soundtrack, which is largely quiet and ambient, but occasionally comes roaring out of its self-contained cage to be a special kind of weird. Hip-hop, throat-singing, dubstep, rock guitar, Chinese opera, all of these coalesce into something more interesting like youâre listening to the most eclectic random-order playlist you can find, yet it all works together and fits. Sometimes a song will grate on you after youâve tried a boss for the 20th time, but it certainly never stops being inventive.

Itâs rare to be as conflicted with a game as I am with Phantom Blade Zero. It is, on paper, exactly what most character action fans would want, but there are just a few choices it makes where I wish someone had shaken the person in charge of making that decision and set them straight, and I canât help but let those things gnaw at me. There are several ways in which this game defies any kind of score I could give it, so Iâm left with just a swirling feeling that we âmerelyâ got a fantastic game with some decisions I think could be changed to create an even better one.

#3739. As Arc Raiders celebrates its first birthday, publisher Nexon reveals the extraction shooter has topped 17 million sales, but revenue is set to decline

Arc Raiders, Embark Studios' popular extraction shooter, has exceeded 17m copies sold, according to publisher Nexon.

Arc Raiders was released at the end of October 2025, so reaching that milestone in a year is nothing to scoff at. According to Nexon's latest earnings report, however, only 1m copies of those 17 were sold in the third quarter - meaning sales have certainly slowed down.

Relatedly, Nexon said it expects Arc Raiders' revenue to decline in the fourth quarter compared to the same period last year - when the game enjoyed its hugely successful launch - and anticipates revenue will be "broadly flat sequentially". Despite this, the company said Arc Raiders' revenue was "within the outlook", naming its Frozen Trail update as a key moment that brought back some lapsed players while introducing new ones.

Indeed, Frozen Trail boosted the game's Steam player count, and reports suggest it also helped Arc Raiders hit a six-month player high across various platforms.

Even with its slowing sales, Arc Raiders remains one of Nexon's most successful titles. The company primarily attributed an overall year-on-year revenue increase, for the nine months ended 30th September, to the game.

Looking ahead, the biggest question hanging over Arc Raiders is whether or not it's going to get a dedicated PvE playlist. Following a successful test earlier this summer, Embark has been coy, and hasn't said whether PvE will return as a permanent feature. Arc Raiders' Chinese version does have a dedicated PvE mode, and executive producer Aleksander Grøndal said he could see both PvP and PvE modes co-existing in the future.

#3737. All boss locations in Fortnite Treasure Hunters

Around the Fortnite Treasure Hunters island, there are quite a few bosses you can find and take on in battle, with new ones arriving on a fairly consistent basis. Various quests challenge you to seek out these foes and take them out in battle, which means you need to know where they spawn.

Tracking down any specific character around the island is tough, even on a mini-sized island like the one present in Treasure Hunters, as there’s lots of ground to explore and plenty of spots they could be hiding. If you’re having trouble tracking them all down, here are all boss locations in Fortnite Treasure Hunters.

As of the time of writing, there are three bosses you can find around the Fortnite Treasure Hunters island. All of them offer a special weapon from the loot pool, alongside some basic drops like ammo and healing items. Here’s a full breakdown of all key details for each one.

Additional bosses may arrive on the island as the mini-season progresses, as there are big weekly updates with loads of new content. If any others are introduced, we’ll add them here.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

The A$AP Rocky boss only ever spawns at The $.$. Rocky location. This key POI is situated near the middle eastern section of the island. At this spot, you can find him wandering around slightly north of the boat, standing on the beachy area nearby.

You can find the Lil Uzi Vert boss hanging around Lil’ Uzi’s Stronghold. This location can be found near the upper northeast corner of the island. He wanders around the area packed with buildings at this spot, so he can be a bit tough to pinpoint.

Buggy spawns at Buggy’s Beachhead, which was previously known as Loot Lagoon prior to his arrival. You can find this POI near the northern middle section of the island. He spawns outside of the large, shark-themed boat parked at this location.

If you visit any of the boss spawn spots and don’t see them there, this means another player found and defeated them first. Each boss can only be fought once per round, so to ensure you don’t miss out on one of these battles, it’s a good idea to head for one of the boss spawn locations straight out of the battle bus.

#3736. Steam now shows average Steam Deck framerates when browsing games, but Valve says it's considering expanding the feature to other hardware

By providing average data for each game, customers now have a more complete picture".

Valve has released a new Steam update that adds Steam Deck framerate data to a game's store page, giving potential buyers an indication of how well a game runs on the handheld.

As per Valve's announcement post, average framerates are now listed in the Steam Deck Compatibility section of a game's store page, but you'll need to click Learn More to see it. Additionally, the feature is only available for games that have been tested for Deck compatibility - those with Verified, Playable, or Unsupported badges - so while it's not a complete list, it still covers thousands of titles.

According to Valve, average framerates are derived from players running the game on their Steam Decks, assuming they've opted in to provide framerate data. And the store widget also includes another helpful addition: a histogram displaying the percentage of data samples. This shows how often a particular framerate has been reported, and is useful in determining if the game's framerate is sporadic, such as due to stutters.

"The current Steam Deck Verified compatibility rating is based on standardised test criteria, but it may not match every customer's bar for acceptable gameplay," Valve explained of the new feature.

"This is especially true around performance - a game with an Unsupported rating due to unstable performance may be considered playable by some customers, and a Verified game may not reach a framerate that some customers prefer to play at. By providing average framerate data for each game, customers now have a more complete picture of how the game performs on Steam Deck and can make more informed purchase and play decisions."

Currently, Steam's framerate data feature only covers performance on Steam Deck, and for a very good reason: Valve's handheld has standardised hardware, so the results will be the same for all players. However, Valve says it intends to provide framerate data for more devices in the future, but it's not clear if that's ever going to include desktop PCs, considering the complex nature of their hardware configurations.

#3735. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time — The Kotaku Review

When I was a very little kid, I went to Disneyland with my parents. I donât remember much about that trip. But I remember visiting Minnie Mouseâs house in the newly built ToonTown, and I remember my mom explaining a joke to me that we saw inside Minnieâs fridge. There were two wheels of cheese. One was labeled âGoudaâ and the other âNot So Gouda.â Once I understood it, I thought it was hilarious, and (apparently) remembered this tiny, specific, incidental detail forever.

I keep hearing friends and colleagues positively describe The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake as a Disney theme park, and I think theyâre onto something. Having revisited multiple Disneys fairly recently, I would readily believe that whoever drew up the plans for its reimagination of Castle Town did so after seeing the castle at Tokyo Disney, centered through archways, ablaze with lights, surrounded by colorful towers and European architecture and cobblestone streets.

But itâs more than just that single snapshot. Iâm not a Disney fiend, and I didnât grow up with Ocarina of Time; I played it for the first time this past January. Even so, the Ocarina of Time remake immediately invokes a powerful feeling of nostalgia in me despite me having nothing in particular to be nostalgic about, in the same way Tokyo Disney did the second that curry popcorn smell hit. Itâs that feeling of being overwhelmed by the density of detail, the care someone took to ensure that everything, all the way down to the items in the fridge or the slight way Link smiles (or doesnât) when he receives a Medallion, is exactly correct. In both situations, that inescapable cartoon fantasy magic overtook me, drawing me back in the second anything resembling cynicism tried to pull me away.

Once, Ocarina of Timeâs Hyrule was considered vastâas big as a video game world conceivably could be. Now, after the soaring heights and dark depths of Tears of the Kingdom, it comes off as small. Quaint. The whole world is, what, equivalent to maybe one major region in Tears? Two, generously? Look, no matter what people proclaim AI will allow them to do or how fantastic GTA 6 ends up being, I struggle to believe you donât lose something in the minute details as you make a video game world more and more massive. Eventually, you start copying and pasting trees and grasses. The houses start to look the same. Thereâs less specificity, less intention. Iâm not saying such games have none! There are so many open-world marvels! But thereâs a reason the Great Plateau remains one of the most memorable and well-regarded segments of Breath of the Wild so many years laterâitâs compact and immaculately designed, down to a microscopic level, in a way that Nintendo or anyone could not have possibly managed for every single corner of the rest of that Hyrule. It takes too long, and you have to have too many people care too much.

So in returning to a world with such a comparatively small scope after years of stretch, stretch, stretching, Nintendo was able to focus its time, talent, and energy on making Ocarina of Time so deliciously, visually dense. You can feel it, in every last corner, every blade of grass. Castle Town has been transformed from some vague polygons and a few Encarta-ass backdrops to a playground stuffed with detail. Every single house, exterior and interior where available, is remarkably different from the next, its intricacies speaking to the sort of person who might live there. One has an elaborate garden, different pots of flowers carefully arranged just as oneâs neighbor might do. Another belongs to a clearly wealthy individual, another place looks a touch shady. I fully believe that Nintendo had a specific character in mind for each one, possibly even characters we will never see.

Everything is like this! The individual tree huts in Kokiri Forest! The elaborate embroidery on womenâs skirts, the subtle pattern differences on menâs poofy pants! How dungeon mechanisms are now fully operational as coherent little machines instead of magic video game platforms! The directional sound, guiding you, siren-like, through the Lost Woods! The dungeons, fleshed out beyond just solid-colored walls into believable complexes with distinct rooms and themes, as if someone had been using them, at one point, for a real purpose (God, the Forest Temple!). Even the foliage is never, ever uniform, but grows in tufts and swaths varying by how much sunlight its space receives, how close it is to water, what foot traffic might be like. Someone thought about every last blade of grass. I believe this. Itâs more than simply saying, âOh, Ocarina of Time is graphically impressive.â It is that. Itâs a genuine, noticeable leap for Nintendo and a shining proof of what the Nintendo Switch 2 is capable of. But more importantly, I believe it to be a testament of what people are capable of when they are given the time, space, energy, and support to really craft something lovingly. The people who made this must love Ocarina of Time. It shows.

Over 25 hours for main quest plus all major sidequests (masks, Biggoron Sword) and 60+ Gold Skulltulas. I will not be gathering all 100 thank you.

Gorgeous. Exhorbitant amounts of visual and written detail. Lovely redone soundtrack including excellent new pieces. Appropriately faithful to original material.

Almost too easy, both because I am an adult now and also because of improved controls. Voice acting and some main story writing a bit juvenile.

It would be rude of me to imply that this level of attention extended only to what we can see. That same intense commitment to specifics is everywhere. I have particular fondness for how it manifests in all the incidental writing, the little throwaway lines of dialogue with random NPCs around Hyrule. More characters have more dialogue than they ever did (especially if you include the Mask of Truth additions as both child and adult Link), and that dialogue is fleshed out with little jokes, hyperspecific details about characters and the world, and tiny nods to Linkâs personality (âDanondorf?â). Itâs genuinely entertaining just to talk to people.

And look, not every detail-based decision works for me. I find the English voice direction (and I do think this is an issue of direction, not acting talent) grating. Several performances (Saria, Ruto, Navi, the Great Deku Tree, and Kaepora Gaebora) sound like theyâre out of a piece of programming for very young children airing at 9am on PBS. I swapped the voices to Japanese halfway through, which solved it for me because I simply could not understand them anymoreâI cannot comment on whether the Japanese performances are actually better or worse. Having gone back and watched some clips of later scenes in English, I believe the worst offenders of these types of conversations are in the first half of the game. I blame much of the early script, which consists of instance after instance of Nintendo clearly being concerned that players new to Ocarina of Time will have no idea what is going on. Everyone insists on sitting Link down and patiently explaining things to him in far more detail than they did in the original, instead of just letting him at it. You may as well have put a giant âHYRULE CASTLE THIS WAYâ banner with big arrows and lights up when Link first arrives in Castle Town, the way most of the NPCs were acting. I am willing to admit that my tolerance for the second act might be in part because I just got used to this tone as time went on, and again, from switching the voices. But I do also think that the second half has significantly better writing, and trusts the player more to explore and sort things out for themselves.

Does Ocarina of Time âhold upâ? Iâve been asked that a lot this year, on the heels of my January playthrough of the original and now as I work through the remake. I donât think thereâs a holistic answer. I appreciated the original for the groundbreaking design work that it was in its combat, camera, dungeons, and two-sided, then-massive world to explore. In 2026, literally none of it is revelatory anymore. Original Ocarina of Time is a relic nowâfun, fascinating, and clever, but still a relic. Itâs good that games have evolved since then. But whatâs funny about a remake is that it naturally smooths out so many of those edges with its modernity that I think it loses something in the translation. Itâs now more obvious than ever that despite its visual density, Hyrule Field is an empty space. There actually isnât that much to do, a bit like the spaces in Disneyland between theme park rides where all you can do is walk and shop. You can argue that space between dungeons leaves room for contemplation, for slowness, but the practical reality is that most people are just going to start fast-traveling the second they can. Once I learned the songs, I barely went out there again.

And this remake is so buttery. The controls are light and mostly intuitive (the return of the item selection wheel can kiss my ass). Link slides through dungeons gracefully, solving puzzle after puzzle with ease. Thereâs no fight to lock onto the target you want to hit, no confusion as you putter around a room trying to angle the camera to figure out where a hidden switch is. Iâve seen hundreds of more complex, more interesting, and more challenging dungeon puzzles in video games over the years, including many in later Zelda games. In Ocarinaâs, I never died, never struggled. Jabu Jabu went from my least favorite dungeon in the original because of how annoying it was to my least favorite dungeon because of how easy and uneventful it was. Like I said, a theme park ride. On rails. I donât have an answer for how Nintendo could have bridged that gap without making an entirely new game.

But I think it also gains something here: a refreshed perspective. Despite its ease, despite the fact that Ocarina of Time in remake form is inventing nothing and surprising no one, it is fun. It is beautiful. It is, at times, moving. Even with no nostalgia to speak of, and full knowledge of the gameâs plot, I couldnât help but feel a swell of emotion when I first looked out on Hyrule Field, when Ruto and Saria became sages, and when Zelda revealed herself at last. Itâs a testament to the excellence of all the pieces of this remake: its excellent cinematography, pacing, sound, look, feel, all of it, that it can still evoke that in me even when my heart is somewhat hardened against it. The incredible lessons these developers have learned over the years that have allowed them to make bigger and bigger Zelda adventures can also be condensed and focused to great effect.Â

The old guard has said it is handing this series off to a new generation of Zelda developers, who might use their work on Ocarina of Time as a learning experience that will allow them to do things their seniors never thought of doing. Iâm excited to see what comes of that. And maybe Iâm a bit relieved, too, to see a game so thoroughly melt away the tension between what is old and what is new. In fantasy worlds like these, thereâs nothing stopping us from having it all.

Grey’s Anatomy is currently in its 23rd season on the 2026 TV schedule, which is still hard to comprehend. Given that the fans are still tuning in, though, no matter what that hospital has been through, it makes sense. While Ellen Pompeo loves Grey’s Anatomy fans, who have been keeping the show on the air for over 20 years, there is just one thing that annoys her. And I can’t say I blame her.

Pompeo starred in Grey’s Anatomy as the titular Dr. Meredith Grey since the very beginning, before ultimately departing as a series regular midway through Season 19. She’s remained on as narrator and executive producer, frequently returning to the halls of Grey Sloan Memorial in a guest capacity. Having been a staple on television for over 20 years, you’d imagine that Pompeo runs into a lot of fans. Unfortunately, it’s not always the greatest experience. The actress told Magic Radio that even though she loves the fans, she’s annoyed by one thing that would honestly annoy me, too:

To be honest, I’m so grateful for the show and so grateful for the fans, and I love them. But to be honest, when people call me Meredith, I do get a little bit annoyed. So I do get a little annoyed with that. I love that you love the show, but just call me by my right name. And everybody’s so nice, and they just say, you know, ‘I love you so much.’ And so, how really can I be upset at that?

I get why people would call celebrities by their characters’ names. You see them as their characters on television or in movies, and in the moment, you spot them and call them by their signature role. That being said, fans should probably be saying the celebrity’s name rather than their character’s, and I am someone who is a stickler for that. I would definitely find that annoying, because you’re meeting the actual person, not the fictional character. They’re two different people.

For a show like Grey’s Anatomy that has been on for over two decades, I can get why it’s especially annoying as people have had 20 years to Meredith Grey’s actual name. That being said, Pompeo doesn’t seem to have any ill will towards the loyal Grey’s Anatomy fans. Sure, she’s annoyed when they don’t call her by her name, but she still loves them anyway. Folks may just want to be a bit more aware of what they say when they meet Pompeo or any other celebrity and make sure you’re getting the name right.

The actress is not on Grey’s Anatomy as much anymore, but whenever she does return to the medical drama, you never know what to expect. It’s always hard to see a Grey’s Anatomy star leave the series, but in Pompeo’s case, she’s simply not a series regular anymore, but is still a recurring actor. Of course, you can’t have Grey’s Anatomy without the Dr. Meredith Grey, so it’s not like the show could wipe the slate completely clean.

As of now, it’s hard to tell how long Grey’s Anatomy will remain on the air, but there doesn’t seem to be any end in sight. Meaning fans will have plenty of time to practice their hellos to Pompeo if they ever meet her so that they can get the name right. If anything, there are 23 seasons of Grey’s Anatomy reminding you who is starring in the series, so that’s a great place to start, and they’re all streaming with a Hulu subscription.

#3733. Marvel Rivals The Acts of Kurt Wagner event guide

Decipher the prophecies to stop catastrophes.

Nightcrawler has finally made his way into Marvel Rivals, and he’s brought with him a fresh event to tackle. The Acts of Kurt Wagner event has been added to the event page with plenty of rewards you can unlock by progressing through it.

Every Marvel Rivals event is unique, with various special mechanics to navigate and lots of exclusive rewards tied to each one. To help you fully work through this one, here’s a complete walkthrough for The Acts of Kurt Wagner event in Marvel Rivals.

To successfully complete The Acts of Kurt Wagner event in Marvel Rivals, you need to work through a total of four event phases, with eight sections to tackle across all of them. Each part of the event comes with two parts: the Prophecy section, which has three missions, and the Disaster Relief portion, which features another three quests that unlock after you check off the Prophecy part.

All tasks tied to this event task you with completing specific objectives while playing in Quick Match, Competitive, Arcade, or Practice vs. AI. The nature of each specific mission varies, but generally includes relatively straightforward goals like dealing a specific amount of damage, landing a certain number of final hits, and completing a required number of matches.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

To unlock additional missions so you can progress through The Acts of Kurt Wagner event, you first need to complete all available unlocked objectives. All tasks in this event unlock progressively, which means you must work through each individual section to gain access to the next part.

Some parts of this event are locked behind a timer, which means even if you get everything done leading up to it, you’ll have to wait for it to be added. All sections that are locked for a specific amount of time have a countdown on them to help you keep track of this.

There are four exclusive rewards you can earn by progressing through The Acts of Kurt Wagner event. You also get to claim two key currencies for checking off missions throughout it. Here’s a breakdown of all prizes.

The Acts of Kurt Wagner event is available to complete from Nov. 13, 2026 to Jan. 15, 2027. This means you have about two months to work through it and claim all available rewards.

Progressing through this event is a great way to check off key tasks that earn you Chrono Tokens to buy season 11 battle pass skins. There are also lots of other events running alongside The Acts of Kurt Wagner, so if you haven’t completed them all, it’s a good idea to get started on them next. #3732. Rockstar kills any hopes of streaming GTA 6 from Xbox to PC, but you can stream it to your old Xbox One if you like

Rockstar Games has today clarified a few remaining details about Grand Theft Auto 6's framerate target and visual settings on PlayStation 5, PS5 Pro and Xbox Series X/S. And as part of the same announcement, the developer revealed a key detail about the game's cloud streaming options.

GTA 6 will be available to stream via Xbox Cloud Gaming. However, this is only possible on Xbox Series X/S consoles, as well as - surprisingly - the last generation console, Xbox One. Notably, that means you can't use Xbox Cloud Gaming to stream to PC, or other devices, despite it being useable there.

You may recall that in early October, a Verge report said Microsoft had acquired exclusive cloud streaming rights for GTA 6, with the understanding being that the game would be available to stream on any XCloud-supported device - as in, to PC as well. Xbox immediately shot down the report, saying GTA 6 "will not be streaming exclusively or to PC".

Perhaps more surprisingly, the cloud-streamed version will be using Series S graphics settings, not those of the more powerful Series X console. Considering the loss in quality inherent in cloud streaming, this will make for a less-than-ideal way of experiencing the game.

Beyond cloud streaming, GTA 6 supports Remote Play on PlayStation and Xbox, so you can stream the game on your local network to any device, from a PS5 or Xbox Series X/S console.

GTA 6 pre-loading is now available across PlayStation and Xbox. The code-in-box physical editions have also started shipping, letting you claim the code and pre-load your copy in time for GTA 6's 19th November launch.

#3731. Nintendo Just Accidentally Got Every Zelda Nerd’s Hopes Up

Nintendo Switch OnlineThe Legend of Zelda

For the last two weeks, an official Nintendo website has erroneously suggested that The Legend of Zelda: A Link Between Worlds is available on Nintendo Switch Online.

[ALBW] Found this on Nintendo's website today, probably doesn't mean anything though. byu/vertexjrpg inzelda

This was shared today by Reddit user vertexjrpg, who posted a screenshot of what they saw. Kotaku was able to confirm that the NSO indicator was there as recently as this morning, and per Wayback Machine was there as far back as November 4, which is when the “History” section of the 40th anniversary website was first added. As of this afternoon, it has been removed. Kotaku has reached out to Nintendo for comment.

Does this mean anything? Probably not. Most likely, this is a case of whoever made this website putting a button that should have gone somewhere else in the wrong place. It happens. But there’s always the minute possibility that this is somehow a sign of something to come. With GameCube and GBA games now viable fodder for NSO inclusion as of the Switch 2, next on the list would be Wii, Wii U, DS, and 3DS. Right now, the only way to (legally, officially) play games on any of these consoles is by owning the physical system, and either a physical copy of a given game or a digital one downloaded from back when their respective online shops were still active. So it’s not exactly easy for a Zelda fan, especially someone coming in more recently with Ocarina of Time, to experience excellent games like A Link Between Worlds.

I’m not optimistic we’ll see 3DS games on NSO any time soon, but I want to believe it is an eventual inevitability, if only so I can go back at will to an awful lot of otherwise inaccessible PokÃ©mon games. As long as I don’t have to sign up for a third, more expensive subscription tier to make it happen.
