Earlier this year, during the Overwatch Spotlight in which Team 4 promised a different approach to managing the live service game, 10 heroes were teased. Five were released straight away, with Sierra, Shion, D.Mon, and Doctrine all being added to the game in subsequent seasons. This has left just one hero for the last season of the year, who also just so happened to be the hero I was most excited about back when the Spotlight was released.

But good things come to those who wait, and now after the better part of a year we finally know more about this final hero. His character design was shown at BlizzCon, which showed him to be omnic detective (my hype was well placed), but now we also know that he'll be joining the DPS class in season 6, although that wasn't always the plan.

"Back at Spotlight—I forget who I was talking to—we said we were going to do a support in season 6," associate game director Alec Dawson said during a stream with Flats and Emongg. "And originally that was the plan. But as things developed as the hero developed, as we got to mechanics, how they matched with the aesthetic, how they matched with who the hero is supposed to be," things changed. The decision was ultimately taken to switch him to the DPS role. "I don't know what else I'm allowed to say," Dawson adds. "I'll let Aaron [Keller, game director] say anything else."

"We'll just spill it all," Keller says, and that he does. "Megan just slacked that we've said enough but there's a couple of other things that I want to say about him. One of the cool things about this, so there was like a bit of a pivot on Hudson (accidentally leaks his name), oh whoops." Well there it is folks: the omnic detective is called Hudson, a cool name for a cool dude, it all checks out.

Hudson's Role Change Explained in #Overwatch 🔎 He was initially planned as a Support hero, but as development progressed, the team realized the core mechanic people loved most fit the DPS role better. The hero set record scores in research groups. https://t.co/VxTMpsPLUrNovember 13, 2026

As a support main I am a little sad to hear about this change to DPS, but seeing as Team 4 explained how they "leaned into the things we loved the most about this hero and it definitely fit DPS a lot better", I'm happy with the change. I'll just have to put support aside for a couple of months, because there's no way I'm missing out on this hero.

This isn't just because he looks cool; according to Keller, Hudson is the most popular hero to-date among their internal and external testers: "We're always testing stuff and we have a user research group here and we'll bring in external players and stuff like that, and this hero by far got the highest scores of any hero that we've tested with these groups. I think he's so much fun."

To put this into perspective, the second most popular hero among testers within the last few years is Juno; a hero I would consider to be one of the best in recent Overwatch history. Her kit is fun, intuitive, and gels with her character design. So if that's the bar Hudson has beaten then my excitement is yet again very well placed. Oh, and Dawson says "he has a very fun accent", which really seals the deal for me.

#3728. Europe is about to get very tough on loot boxes in games, according to a leaked draft of the landmark Digital Fairness Act

"The digital era has fundamentally transformed consumer experiences..."

An alleged draft of the potentially game-changing Digital Fairness Act has leaked ahead of its scheduled publication tomorrow (11th November), containing proposals that could dramatically affect the way games operate and are monetised within the European Union.

The draft, published by French publication Contexte (via Video Games Industry Memo) goes as far as to recommend that loot boxes (uncertainty-based rewards) be turned off by default for minors, as well as the sale of in-game items and currencies. There's also a recommendation that all players - not just minors - should be able to turn off offers related to these lootboxes and gambling mechanics.

"The digital era has fundamentally transformed consumer experiences," the draft of the Digital Fairness Act begins. "It has enabled faster, more convenient and wider access to an ever-increasing range of goods and services. At the same time, it has given rise to new and more sophisticated ways of influencing consumers' choices.

"Along with the indisputable benefits in choice and efficiency, the extensive use of digital technologies allows both old and new unfair commercial practices to affect consumers at scale, exacerbating risks to their economic interests, as well as to their mental and physical wellbeing. Vulnerable consumers are particularly affected."

The Digital Fairness Act calls for greater transparency around a "transactional decision". Which means: "Price transparency on the real value of in-app purchases using virtual currencies and the probabilities of winning for virtual offers with uncertainty-based rewards (loot boxes).

"All consumers can turn off virtual offers with uncertainty-based rewards. Some spending-maximising practices prohibited for minors, with the remaining turned off by default. Supporting self-regulation for video games and legal obligation for video games to have an age-appropriate rating. All consumers can turn off attention-maximising features, with some prohibited for minors and the remaining turned off by default."

"Spending-maximising" refers to systems that pressure us to spend more money than we want to, such as reward systems or pay-to-progress or pay-to-win systems. They're all being targeted here, as is virtual currency, which provides a layer of abstraction as to the real cost of goods.

"It may be difficult for minors to resist such perceived pressure to pay," the Digital Fairness Act said with regard to progression-linked systems. "Therefore, where a product is directed at minors or when the trader is aware with reasonable certainty that the product is used by minors, pay-to-progress or pay-to-win mechanisms [...] should not be made available to minors."

The Digital Fairness Act is a forthcoming European legislative proposal designed to update consumer protection rules for various digital dangers that we face today. Importantly, it's not law yet, and it has iterations and discussions to go through before it will be. A timeline on the Digital Fairness Act explainer website suggests it could be adopted late in 2027, then applied more broadly by 2030.

It's also hoping to tackle many things besides shady video game monetisation, including "problematic" influencer marketing, "unfair" pricing practices - such as obscuring the real cost of something until you've progressed through layers trying to buy it - and mysterious-sounding "dark patterns". These relate to 'easy to sign-up, hard-to-cancel' processes, it seems.

These changes aren't happening in a vacuum. Earlier this year, the well-known European age-rating body PEGI announced historic alterations to its game-rating criteria, with an eye to better categorising the dangers of loot box-containing games and aggressively monetised games. These changes have already started to roll out and mean that a game like EA Sports FC, which was previously routinely rated PEGI 3, now automatically gets a PEGI 16 rating because of its Ultimate Team card pack (loot box) system.

The effect of the Digital Fairness Act could tip the balance against these systems being included in games at all. Expect more discussion and digestion of the proposed changes as the Act is officially published tomorrow.

#3727. How to unlock Flounder and Sebastian in Disney Dreamlight Valley The Keepsake Sea

The collection of characters from The Little Mermaid is growing, with Ariel’s beloved fish friends Flounder and Sebastian joining the village in Disney Dreamlight Valley. The process for unlocking them looks vastly different from all other villagers, though, and can be tricky to navigate.

If you’re hoping to get every character available to find and meet around the valley, figuring out what needs to be done to recruit these two is essential. Here’s how to unlock Flounder and Sebastian in Disney Dreamlight Valley.

Flounder and Sebastian can be unlocked by purchasing either the Deluxe Edition or the Ultimate Edition of The Keepsake Sea in DDV. These two Adventure Companions are exclusive content locked behind these special variants of the Expansion Pass, which means you must buy one of the two to get them.

With either of these versions purchased, you’ll then be able to unlock Flounder and Sebastian in DDV. These two are likely locked behind a few quests, probably ones that require you to first unlock Ariel and progress through part of The Keepsake Sea’s storyline to learn about Adventure Companions. We’ll provide an update here on all additional unlock requirements once they’re available to tackle.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Flounder and Sebastian will very likely only ever be available as exclusive bonus content unlocked for purchasing either the Deluxe Edition or the Ultimate Edition of The Keepsake Sea DLC. Most other DLCs have had similar exclusivity systems for special game editions, like Sven as an exclusive mount with the Deluxe Edition of Wishblossom Ranch.

All items included in special editions have never been available in any other way. This system has been in place for years, so it’s unlikely to change in the future. This means that the only way to get Flounder and Sebastian in your valley is by buying one of the two DLC game versions that include them.

Flounder and Sebastian are Adventure Companions, not full-on villagers in DDV. This means they act as a hybrid between a Companion and a villager. These special Companions can be given gifts, have daily discussions, and come with their own set of rewards, but are not quite as built out as villagers.

#3726. He Was Just A Boy

I think most kids wish they could grow up fast. They want to be free of the rules their parents set for them that feel arbitrary and unfair, and theyâre often told âwhen youâre older, you can make your own rules.â When I was in elementary school playing The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the first time, I was young enough that Linkâs seven-year slumber seemed like a dream come true. No longer would he, and by extension myself, be restrained by his small stature. Oh the adventures weâd go on and monsters weâd face. Oh how naive I was.

Itâs been years since I revisited Ocarina of Time, and while Iâd always known the series to be tinged with melancholy, one thing that nearly 30 years of distance from the original Nintendo 64 game has given me is an understanding that Ocarina of Time is a tragedy. The Hero of Time wins the day and saves Hyrule, but at a great cost of his own innocence. You can put the Master Sword back into its pedestal and go back to your childhood, but youâll never erase the horrors of seeing every safe haven you once knew desecrated beyond recognition while youâre still carrying the heart and soul of a child, even as your body grows older and stronger.

If youâve already played Ocarina of Time, the lead-up to the eventual time skip in the remake feels dreadful in a way that even all the childlike whimsy happening around Link canât cure. On top of young Linkâs appearance being much more expressive and youthful than it was on the Nintendo 64, there are a bunch of small details in dialogue that make it clear this is a little baby pushed out of the nest. Little dude calls the king of all evil âDanondorf,â is three apples tall, and has the resting pout of a baby who doesnât cover his mouth when he coughs. This isnât the classical vision of a hero, itâs a wide-eyed baby who slaps around wooden sticks with his friends in a playground, imitating the heroic soldiers theyâve been told tall tales of in just the few years theyâve been able to walk.

As you grow older, you learn that those tales of heroism arenât all theyâre chalked up to be. Many still make the decision to reach for the sword, but in Ocarina of Time, Link doesnât get to make that decision, it is thrust upon him at an age when his whole understanding of what being a hero means would be shaped by those simple childhoodÂ  stories. The realities of being a hero canât be understood by a mere child, and thatâs why he is forcibly aged up seven years: so that he can wield the sword he was destined to carry and defeat an evil no one else can.

The concept of âstolenâ lives comes up throughout Ocarina of Time, though many of the people who are âdestinedâ to save the world take comfort in the sense of purpose they find in becoming a pawn in the grand design. Many of the Sages say this to Link directly; though they canât return to the family and friends they once knew, it brings them joy to know they are part of something bigger than themselves. Link, on the other hand, who has been dragged into this as a child with no time to grow up and decide for himself, is treated as a tragic figure, one that Zelda sends back to his childhood in the hopes that he can live out the life he deserved. If only it were that simple. At the very least, the Ocarina of Time remake makes that terrible fate more clear. Rather than just pointing out that Link has aged up, Rauru, the Sage of Light, breaks the news to Link that he has lost seven years, expressing this with remorse, rather than simply as a matter of fact.Â

Iâm curious to see if Nintendo does end up remaking Majoraâs Mask, the even-more-woeful sequel set after Ocarina of Time in this new timeline where Link is able to live out his childhood, only to be haunted by his own forgotten heroics. Thatâs the trade-off in saving the timeline: if youâve done it right, no one will ever know what you did. This version of Link lives out his days saving Hyrule and then Termina, once again having to rely on time travel and constant repetition to be the hero the people need, only for all his efforts to be washed away in the unforgiving waves of time.

All that regret keeps his tortured soul alive for centuries, living on as a Heroâs Shade the player meets in Twilight Princess, wishing anything heâd done could have been remembered, and that he could see the fruits of his labor memorialized in anything tangible. Perhaps, if he cannot be remembered as a hero, everything he learned in these invisible lives can be passed down to someone who can be. Thus, he teaches the Link of Twilight Princess skills that help him defeat Ganondorf in his own timeline, ensuring that even if everything heâd done has been forgotten, it will live on in future generations. Centuries later, the Hero of Time is still protecting his inner child, because even if he has finally been able to age as he should have, he canât let go of all that he was forced to watch unfold in his multiple childhoods.

The Zelda series has always been replete with somber stories, and while theyâve often been communicated subtly and left for fans to theorize about, lore bibles and official materials have turned theories into reality. Legends that were once only talked about in dedicated forums in the early 2000s have become text, written on the record and accepted as Hyrule history. It can sometimes be exhausting seeing theories âconfirmedâ and made canon, as the incessant need for every piece of lore to be documented in online databases has robbed so many stories of their color, their room for inference and interpretation, in favor of black-and-white facts on a page. But itâs good to see that the Ocarina of Time remake treats the tragedy that is the Hero of Timeâs many lives with the gravity it deserves.

#3725. Rockstar details Grand Theft Auto 6 PS5 Pro enhancements, but it'll still only run at 30FPS

Pushing consoles to "their absolute limits".

As Grand Theft Auto 6 preloads go live, developer Rockstar has detailed the enhancements coming to the PS5 Pro version of the game, confirming these won't include framerates above the 30 FPS its targeting for consoles.

Rockstar shared the news in a blog post released to announce that GTA 6 pre-loading is now available ahead of its release date on 19th November.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 has been fully developed from the ground up to provide the best possible experience for the current generation of consoles," Rockstar says. It goes on to reconfirm GTA 6 is targeting 30 FPS on all consoles, saying the game is pushing modern machines "to their absolute limits" in order to "bring the vast and rich world of Leonida to life — while maintaining the density and visual fidelity of all its environments and inhabitants."

PS5 players can expect high-fidelity haptic feedback through the DualSense controllers, improved spatial audio, and Tempest 3D audio, while PS5 Pro enhancements come in the form of PSSR support and ray tracing shadows, which should make the game look especially fancy, plus improved load times. PlayStation players can also expect remote play support. As for the Xbox, the post clarified details on Xbox Cloud Gaming, which will allow the game to be streamed to Xbox consoles including the Xbox One. Notably, this won't work on PC.

Grand Theft Auto 6's 30 FPS target was previously confirmed by Rockstar back in August, but there was some uncertainty around a possible 60fps performance mode at the time. Still, those PS5 technical boons do a lot of work to improve the games it's applied to, which if nothing else should mean GTA 6 will be quite the looker.

Spoilers for Season 3, Episode 3 of Rings of Power are ahead! You can stream the first four episodes with an Amazon Prime subscription.

At the end of Rings of Power Season 2, The Stranger finally realized his name was Gandalf. Now, in Season 3 of The Lord of the Rings prequel, he’s really starting to look like the wizard we know and love. That became especially true in Episode 3, which was part of a four-episode premiere on the 2026 TV schedule, because Gandalf finally got his hat. So, in honor of this monumental moment, I asked Daniel Weyman about putting on such an iconic piece of his costume, and he told me the deeper meaning behind it.

Of course, those of us who love The Lord of the Rings movies associate Gandalf with his robe, staff and big hat. Now, in The Rings of Power, he has all of that. Weyman explained during an interview with CinemaBlend that talking to audiences about this really hammers home the notion that he’s portraying a version of the character Ian McKellen also famously played on screen. Meanwhile, within the story, Gandalf has no clue about the significance and history of that hat. However, it still carries significant meaning to him, as Weyman explained:

What did Gandalf want to do with that hat? Well, he just had this argument with Tom Bombadil, a really serious argument, as it turns out, where Tom Bombadil has disappeared when he comes back. And how does that sit with Gandalf? And then, when this hat magically sort of rolls down to his feet, the final thing, the last vestige of Tom Bombadil in the hut, and Gandalf knows his purpose is to go through the desert, which nearly killed him [in] Season 2.

At the beginning of Season 3, Gandalf is hanging out with Tom Bombadil, and as Weyman said, they get into an argument. After that, the wizard finds The Secret Fire, learns about the other wizards who were sent to Middle-earth, and he becomes aware of the fact that his mission is to help save the Dark Wizard. When he returns to Tom Bombadil’s hut, Tom is gone, and a hat blows over to Gandalf. According to Daniel Weyman, through all this, his character realizes it's time to go back through the desert.

However, there’s more to this. According to the actor, getting this hat is also a symbol of friendship, and it’s part of his armor. Tom Bombadil left this for him, and it helps Gandalf realize his mission and come to terms with the fact that he’s not alone:

He finds that this hat is both a piece of his friendship, but it's also a piece of his armor, and he puts it on. He feels the sun beat down on his head, and he has to put it on because the desert's dangerous. And so, weirdly, in that moment, yes, we're all going to see the outline of it and understand what that means for us, because we know about Gandalf in our world. But for him, he now feels like he's more complete, because he's got another friend to go on a journey with, because he's got another piece of his soft armory.

Weyman went on to tell me that the “key” for him while playing such an iconic character is to “stay present with” his story. He also noted that whether you consider the hat’s history or not, this moment did help Gandalf feel “more complete.”

Now, if you’d like to see how this transformation continues, you can catch the next two episodes of Rings of Power’s third season on Wednesday, November 18.

#3722. Ads are coming to Xbox Cloud Gaming, and an executive thinks this is the only way to avoid ‘dramatic’ price increases in the industry

Advertisements in subscription services are nothing new. Netflix, Amazon, and every other company out there has some sort of ad-supported tier, which is often way cheaper or even entirely free depending on the service and how aggressive the ads are. However, gaming is a different beast, and we companies haven’t found ways to implement them outside the mobile space, where they remain on a quid-pro-quo basis anyway.

But that is slowly changing with the prevalence of subscriptions, and Xbox Cloud Gaming has just received an ad-based free edition players can hop onto without paying a single dime. Xbox Cloud Gaming has long been in decline and probably quite expensive for Microsoft to run and sustain, which led to time limits implemented across every Game Pass tier. With ads, things could turn the tide on Microsoft’s cloud gaming service and, according to Xbox general manager Jonathan Stringfield, potentially avert inevitable price hikes throughout the industry.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Stringfield predicts that, in the coming years, the games industry will inevitably be faced with rising costs and sustainability issues, which will then produce “dramatic” results whereby the costs will be offloaded to the end-user.

“Either of two things need to happen if we want to stick with the model as it exists today: We either need to dramatically increase the price of games, which I don’t think would be terribly popular with folks, or we need to find other mechanisms to allow access,” Stringfield said to Games Beat. One of these “other mechanisms” is, of course, ads.

“When we talk about advertising—and things that are adjacent to it that amount to recurrent revenue, whether it’s subscriptions or otherwise—what this allows for is an alternative,” he explained.

Stringfield prefaced these comments by saying advertising definitely cannot work in every game and probably not even every console or platform, and it isn’t necessarily going to be hammered into everything under the sun. However, they are to be viewed as a potential way to offset costs without extracting more money out of the end-user via higher prices. The very existence of premium platforms, and quite popular ones at that, whose sole stated purpose is to delete ads, does run counter to this somewhat.

People are very obviously willing to pay not to see ads or be interrupted during their viewing or gaming, so it remains to be seen if or how advertisements can be used in gaming broadly, outside of the limited scope of ad-based subscription services. Maybe we will all end up on the cloud eventually (Sam Altman does seem keen on the idea) and thus be forced to watch ads and, like Sony’s patent says, even be made to stand up and scream the product’s name on the screen to be given the ability to continue.

Grim ideas, and I hope they never come true.

#3721. Grand Theft Auto 6 becomes the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation Store history

UPDATE: And the most pre-ordered game in Xbox Store history.

UPDATE 11TH NOVEMBER: Grand Theft Auto 6 has also become the most pre-ordered game "of all time" on the Xbox Store, Microsoft has announced. And on that platform, again, the advice is to pre-load because of "unprecedented demand" for the game, a post on Xbox Wire said.

The Xbox difference is that you can use Xbox Cloud to stream GTA 6 to other Xbox devices, although not PC, notably - the game isn't available on PC and presumably Rockstar doesn't want it playable there by any means. Microsoft's stream-deal with Rockstar has also expanded to include Red Dead Redemption 2 "and more", which will be available to stream in the "coming months".

ORIGINAL STORY 10TH NOVEMBER: Sony has just announced that Grand Theft Auto 6 has become "the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store". Note, it's not the most pre-ordered game in PlayStation history, just on its digital PlayStation Store.

The announcement, which comes as Sony prepares to ditch physical releases for an all-digital future, was made in a PlayStation Blog post confirming pre-loads for GTA 6 are now live.

"Grand Theft Auto 6 is now the most pre-ordered game in the history of PlayStation Store," Sony wrote. "Given this unprecedented demand, we've joined with Rockstar Games to allow players to start pre-loading the game nine days early, so they're ready to play on launch day.

"We strongly advise that everyone who is hoping to play on launch day to pre-load the game as soon as possible," the blog post added. So: consider yourselves advised.

GTA 6 becomes available as soon as your region's clock ticks over from midnight into 19th November, which, if you're in New Zealand, means you'll play the game before everyone else. If only there were a way to pretend you lived there...

Elsewhere in the blog post, Sony underlined some features coming specially to GTA 6 on PS5 and PS5 Pro. On Xbox, meanwhile, cloud streaming is supported, but not - sadly - to PC.

Last night, in a Take-Two financial earnings call, company leader Strauss Zelnick said pre-orders for GTA 6 are tracking "far above expectations" and that soon, "numbers will speak for themselves". Presumably because they will be gripped by an excited form of sentience. It's expected that GTA 6 could become the best-selling instalment in an already mega-selling series; Zelnick reckons GTA 6 will "set a new baseline" for Take-Two in terms of success.

Have you managed to resist pre-ordering it yet?

With its strong build, consistent connectivity and great modular features, this is the best 8BitDo pad I've had the pleasure of using, but it's not worth the money when comparable and even better-specced controllers are near half the price.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

Pricing has remained the elephant in the room for almost all PC Gaming hardware this year, but when it comes to controllers, you don't even have the memory crisis to blame.

And yet, I feel similarly about the 8BitDo Ultimate 3E as I do all that memory-equipped hardware: This is genuinely an excellent gamepad that I have loved reaching for every day, but that price stings so badly that it becomes quite hard to recommend.

Unless, of course, you really want a dual-compatible (Xbox and PC) modular wireless controller.

✅ You want the best wireless pad for your Xbox: The Ultimate 3E acts exactly like the standard Microsoft Xbox controller, even waking up the console with the on button, except it's better in almost every way.

❌ You want the best value for money: You can get the GameSir G7 Pro, with its tri-mode connectivity and charging stand for nearly half the price. Add ten bucks to the G7 Pro, and you can even get its 8K variant.

With its strong build, consistent connectivity and great modular features, this is the best 8BitDo pad I've had the pleasure of using, but it's not worth the money when comparable and even better-specced controllers are near half the price.

Tri-mode for PC and Xbox. Bluetooth for Mobile

This isn't just a PC controller that works wired on an Xbox, like most controllers. This is an officially licensed product with Microsoft's coveted wireless chip inside, meaning it works wirelessly on Xbox and PC. Not only that, but it even wakes up the Xbox when you click the On button, effectively doing what the standard Xbox controller does. This may not seem like a big deal, but it's shockingly rare among third-party controller manufacturers right now.

To swap between PC and Xbox, you just have to swap the adapter between the two. Given the price, I'd really love two adapters, as the Turtle Beach Stealth Pro II has, but it's not a huge pain, and the controller has Bluetooth and wired connectivity.

In addition to coming with a charging dock, carry case, and USB Type-A to Type-C cable, the case comes with spare thumbsticks, face buttons, and a D-pad. That's because the Ultimate 3E is modular. You can take off the faceplate and swap around the parts above in mere moments. It's intuitive, and all the parts are built well.

You also get more modern controller upgrades, like TMR joysticks, two buttons at the back and two extra buttons on top. It does do away with some of my criticisms of the 8BitDo Pro 3 by giving you a 1,000 Hz polling rate and an aux jack, but even then, I would have hoped for 8,000 Hz at this price point. Admittedly, most players won't use 8,000 Hz polling given its battery-sucking ways, but you'd still expect a pro-level controller to have everything thrown at it.

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The main difference between the Ultimate 3 and Ultimate 3E is that the 3E comes with RGB rings around the sticks, has rubberised grips at the front and back, and, of course, modular parts. The 3E is also heavier.

As far as modularity is concerned, it's very easy to do. For the thumbsticks and D-pad, you can simply pull them until they pop off, and then slot in the replacement. The face buttons are a little more involved, with you needing to take the faceplate off, pinch the two sides of the face button module and pull. From here, you can swap with the included face button module in the carry case, which is identical except it comes with mechanical switches.

It seems unlikely you will use this modularity every day, but this level of customisation is certainly welcome to me, and does make the controller feel unique. Unfortunately, though, it doesn't opt for any peculiar modules, like the Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded, which does feel like a slightly wasted opportunity.

Given it works on PC and Xbox, I'd love a touchpad module option. The Victrix even gives you the option to change the stick layout, which the Ultimate 3E doesn't. There are levels of modularity on controllers, and the Pro BFG Reloaded is one level above.

At 285 grams, the 8BitDo Ultimate 3E is around 10 grams lighter than the standard Xbox controller, and it feels super sturdy and comfortable in the hands. The Ultimate 3 and 3E are slightly larger than the Ultimate 2, and I can comfortably say this is the sweetest 8BitDo controller I've held. It's impeccably well-balanced and smoothly slots into my palms. All of its buttons are easy to get to, and surprisingly, I even found myself using the two extra buttons near the bumpers. 8BitDo clearly knows how to make a great-feeling controller.

If I really shake it, the controller has a slight rattle in the centre, but I never heard that in the course of usual play.

The Ultimate 3E has been my pad of choice whilst trying to collect the Fortnite Pirate Token, and I may not have gotten the loot, but I have managed to achieve a tonne of kills. It's not failed me once in its connectivity; buttons are snappy and precise, and it doesn't fatigue me after hours of bad luck in the game.

More recently, it's been my way of playing Warhammer Survivors, a very chill game where you constantly hold down the thumbsticks, and these TMR sticks are impressive—precise and smooth.

The best word I can use to describe the Ultimate 3E is clean. Well, not after my hands get on it, but we'll get to that later. The 3E comes in a suave black model, with almost every element of the pad being a shade of black. The only thing cutting through that lack of colour is the LED around the on button and the RGB sticks. Simply click the start button to turn on the RGB, and hold it while using the D-pad to change colour, vibrancy and mode.

It reminds me of a souped-up version of Nintendo's Pro Controller, and that is a big compliment in my eyes. The Ultimate 3 does have some gorgeous colourways, but if you want something simple yet pretty, the 3E is great.

The same can be said for the stand, which is all black with a small RGB strip which doubles as a way of telling you if your controller is charging.

However, there is one blemish here: the grips can get grubby. I've been using GameSir's G7 Pro 8K for almost half a year now and I haven't managed to get its grips quite as mucky looking at the 3E. It certainly doesn't look awful with a speck of dust or grime on the grip, but it does look less clean in both senses of the word.

For the Ultimate 3E, 8BitDo uses the Ultimate Software X, which is the same software it uses for Xbox devices. This is mildly annoying as I use the standard Ultimate software for my Retro keyboard and Retro R8 gaming mouse, meaning I can't use one bit of software for all three.

With this software, you can customise the range and rumble of the triggers, the deadzone of sticks, and get firmware updates. It's fairly straightforward, though after the initial setup, you can do most of the everyday customising without software, including setting controls to the extra buttons, adjusting RGB, and even changing volume.

The 1400 mAh battery gets around 18 hours of play before it needs to charge again. That's fine. It's not especially big, but it's not minuscule either. However, I have never once needed to consciously charge the controller, because the stand is just the natural place I'd put the controller at the end of the day. The stand looks pretty, and I've never managed to place it at such an odd angle that the controller won't charge. I have, on many occasions, very haphazardly slotted it on top, and it's been ready to go the next day.

The benefit of this charging stand is that it has a hidden compartment underneath to slot the 2.4 GHz connector, meaning it works as both a charging stand and receiver.

If you are looking for something like the Xbox Elite Controller that works wirelessly on Xbox, the Ultimate 3E is basically 8BitDo's imitation, but cheaper. And that seems to be the main sell, here.

However, if you are simply looking for a great wireless controller for your PC with solid specs and a great feel, it's significantly more expensive than the comparably good GameSir G7 Pro. In fact, the GameSir G7 Pro 8K even outpaces it for PC competitive performance thanks to a polling rate that is eight times higher.

As such, there's only one specific niche for which I could wholeheartedly recommend the Ultimate 3E, and that's if you are primarily an Xbox gamer in need of a wireless controller. But for the average PC Gamer, the Ultimate 3E, even with its neat modular functions and sweet feel, is $50 more than I'd happily pay.

One thing I can say is that it has replaced every other controller when it comes to my Xbox, and that is somewhat of a win for 8BitDo, even if it feels like a begrudging one at $150.

With its strong build, consistent connectivity and great modular features, this is the best 8BitDo pad I've had the pleasure of using, but it's not worth the money when comparable and even better-specced controllers are near half the price.

James is a more recent PC gaming convert, often admiring graphics cards, cases, and motherboards from afar. In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

As we drift closer to the release of GTA 6, set for next Thursday, we’re seeing levels of marketing unheard of before. Take-Two chief Strauss Zelnick warned us about Rockstar’s innovative marketing tactics, but never in my life would I have expected a full-blown animated TV show set in-universe.

As shared by Discussing Film on X, Rockstar Games has made an entire animated TV show called MACCA & FRIENDS, which follows Macca the Gator getting into all kinds of trouble in the state of Leonida. It is an in-universe TV show, meaning you will be able to watch it on GTA 6‘s fictional WEAZEL TV network (also appearing in GTA 5) and that it will be incorporating in-universe elements such as the mentioned state of Leonida (GTA‘s version of Florida). "A raucous, absurd spin-off that manages to still feel like a first-rate Yakuza game despite the leftfield setting and delightfully unhinged plot," wrote Matt Elliott in Eurogamer's Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii review.

Meanwhile, Atomfall - Rebellion's quirky British take on a Fallout-like post-apocalyptic idea - was awarded three out of five stars. "If you can get over a difficult start and fancy a lean take on the survival genre, Atomfall delivers an intriguing tale worth discovering," Tom Orry wrote in Eurogamer's Atomfall review. It's presumably been significantly patched and smoothed since then.

The Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake also scored three out of five stars. "Some excellent enhancements make this the ultimate version of Dragon Quest 3, but it could still do more to make it wholly welcoming to newcomers," Daniella Lucas wrote in Eurogamer's Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D review.

We didn't review Hell Let Loose, but the popular World War 2 shooter would go on to amass a serious following and spawn a follow-up game in Hell Let Loose: Vietnam recently, which we did review. "The lavish jungles, rigid command structure, and emphasis on communication make Hell Let Loose: Vietnam a fascinating war simulator when it works. But its many variables can all too easily devolve into a miserable snipe-fest," Rick Lane wrote.

There's plenty to be getting on with, then.

Sony also announced in the PlayStation Blog post it's retiring the PS Plus app on PC from 10th December. Why? Because nobody really uses it.

"With a very small number of eligible PlayStation Plus Premium members (less than 0.4 percent) using the PlayStation Plus app on PC, making this change allows us to focus on enhancing high-quality experiences that more of our members want to use," Sony wrote. "As a result, the PlayStation Plus cloud streaming app on PC will no longer be available."

#3717. PlayStation's embattled shooter Fairgames has finally been cancelled, a new report says, as live service push withers away

After years of silence, we finally know the fate of PlayStation's embattled live service game Fairgames. The Haven-developed co-op heist shooter has been cancelled, with the silver lining that the studio is not closing down or laying off staff.

According to a new Bloomberg report, the decision to cancel Fairgames was made following the results of a recent playtest. Sony told staff on Tuesday of the playtest's poor reception and of its decision to end development.

"While the test demonstrated strong operational excellence, live ops readiness and community engagement, player feedback and retention results were mixed and fell short of the goals we had set," executives Sean Decker and John Doyle reportedly wrote in an email to staff.

"Combined with challenging market conditions in the PvP shooter genre, we have made the difficult decision to cease development on the game."

A PlayStation spokesperson later confirmed that developers at Haven will now support other teams within the PlayStation Studios group, as they continue to "explore new creative opportunities".

Fairgames was initially announced in 2023 as one of several in-development live service games, as part of an initiative by former PlayStation boss Jim Ryan to create more than a dozen games that generate recurring revenue.

Most of those titles were cancelled before they were even revealed, and those that made it out, such as Concord, flopped severely. Even Sony darling Guerrilla Games seemingly can't make it work, with recent reports saying the studio's Horizon Hunters Gathering - initially envisioned as a live service spin on the robo dinosaur series - will now shift into a more traditional co-op structure without live service elements. That's assuming the team can show a revamped version of the game to executives by December.

The news of Fairgames' cancellation isn't surprising. The game has had a tumultuous development journey ever since its reveal. Initially set for release in 2025, the game was soon pushed back to 2026, following the departure of studio founder Jade Raymond.

Though Sony later reiterated its commitment to its remaining in-development live service titles, Fairgames was never shown to the public again. That same year, game director Daniel Drapeau left Haven - another key departure suggesting the game had difficulties and might not see release.

Throughout that time, Fairgames has reportedly been reworked multiple times, with a plan for it to be re-revealed under a new name. That name is believed to be Break In, linked to a trademark Sony filed in May, but with the project cancelled, we may never know if that was the case.

#3716. ‘The name’s Cullen. Edward Cullen’: Robert Pattinson reportedly top choice for next James Bond

It'll be exciting to see how he pulls it off if selected.

Bond. James Bond. Two words. Two syllables. Sharp, striking, piercing your chest as soon as they are uttered. They mean a lot to many, and every so often they are thrown into the ether, like a phonetic parasite seeking their next host. Who will carry them for the next year, two, five, a decade? A hard question to answer.

But according to a new rumor, Robert Pattinson is the top choice to embody Ian Fleming’s womanizer spy, with Amazon MGM reportedly considering him their favorite for the role. As first reported by Matthew Belloni in Puck (via The Guardian), Pattinson was given “favorable contract terms” to play this legendary character, which would see him star in three movies rather than the four expected of other candidates. The actor would also be paid significantly more, which signals how keen Amazon MGM is to get his face and name associated with the brand and character.

Read what’s behind the latest news in gaming (with a bit of snark) by subscribing to the Destructoid Checkpoint newsletter!

Previously, it was claimed Callum Turner was in the running for Bond going forward, according to Deadline, with Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor also putting themselves up. That outlet did say four offers were sent out but managed to confirm just these three, and it would appear now that Pattinson was the ultimate contender.

Now, if you asked me, I’d say Turner was, at least in terms of physical appearance and stature (which, of course, is almost just as important as actual acting skills for a character like James Bond) suits the character much more than Pattinson. The latter practically kills every role involving strange, mysterious, and at times evidently neurodivergent characters, and while he did nail the strong, silent stoic in 2022’s The Batman, I still fail to see how he could handle a highly sexualized, outgoing, womanizer Bond.

However, Daniel Craig’s Bond was markedly different than what we were used to. He had a lot more depth and a broad, emotionally charged backstory that fundamentally altered how he behaved. The core tenets of the character remained intact, though Craig did give them somewhat of a sociopathic tone.

How Pattinson will play the character and what flair he will end up giving him remains to be seen, but I’m confident enough in his acting skills to believe just enough that he can actually pull it off.

#3715. New York City, Mayor Mamdani to host youth game dev contest to help boost local game industry growth

The home locale of Rockstar Games’ corporate headquarters is trying to invest in further game development locally, thanks in large part to a certain popular mayor and his office.

Today, New York City and Mayor Zohran Mamdani announced NYC Game Jam, a two-day youth competition for game development in which young New Yorkers “design and build a video game around a set theme,” according to a report by Variety. It will take place this weekend.

But don’t expect a return to Liberty City here. The competition’s theme is “Get There Already,” focused on the city’s transit, and according to the Mayor’s Office of Media and Entertainment, “participants will build a game about getting across the city” and “every game must be about transit or the experience of getting around a city, suitable for all ages, and free of violence, weapons, and other illicit activity.” No grand theft here.

The office also said that NYC’s gaming sector lists “about 7,900 jobs across approximately 380 firms and generates $2.6 billion in annual economic impact,” so this competition is an effort to continue that trend and keep games being developed in the city.

“Whether you’re exploring the forests of Hyrule or riding across the frontier at Nuevo Paraíso, video games invite us into worlds born from the imagination of their designers. And that creativity represents an enormous opportunity here in New York City,” Mamdani said. “As the industry grows, we want to make sure the next generation of game developers and designers can build their futures right here at home. This Game Jam is a chance to open the door to that industry for young New Yorkers, connect them with the people shaping it, and give them the tools and support to turn their biggest ideas into careers.”

A panel of industry veterans will select three finalists in the contest, with first place winning $3,000, second place $1,500, and third place $500, with the winnings to be split amongst all members of the game-making teams. It’s unclear if generative AI will be allowed in the contest.

As a native New Yorker, this excites me. I’d love more studios to work out of Manhattan rather than California, selfishly, because it’s less travel for me.

We’re over halfway through the 2026 fall TV schedule, and I need to talk about one unexpected highlight in my weekly viewing. This season has been full of exciting TV, from the exciting competition on ABC mainstay Dancing With The Stars or finding a new favorite in CBS’s Eternally Yours, but it feels like no one’s talking about NBC’s Newlyweds, and that’s a problem.

Newlyweds is a new comedy show starring Tea Leoni, Tim Daly and Jamie Lee Curtis, and guys, I kind of love it. It’s nothing groundbreaking, but that’s one reason why I appreciate it it. It feels like a classic sitcom from the ‘90s like The Nanny, Will & Grace or Frasier that just don't get made anymore. It’s about two middle-aged people, Jeanie and James, who fall in love, and decide to quickly get married. They are pretty much opposites, but love each other enough to merge their different lives despite it. It’s like watching an ongoing romantic comedy with a mix of humor and earnestness.

Jamie Lee Curtis plays James’ meddling ex-wife Claudia, who’s always showing up at the worst times to annoy them, and I love how audacious her character is. While the whole thing is pretty formulaic, it’s also comfortingly funny, and I genuinely look forward to watching the next one every week. New episodes follow Happy’s Place every Friday night before dropping for those with a Peacock subscription every Saturday.

The stress of getting into a new show is always the fear of cancellation, and I’m seeing signs for Newlyweds already. For one, when I looked into the TV show itself, I learned that its showrunner, Gail Lerner, was fired from her own series due to “creative differences” a few weeks before the premiere, as reported by THR. The Connors producer Bruce Helford was promptly hired to take over, but issues like this so early in a show’s life is concerning.

The TV Ratings Guide also predicts the show “leans cancellation” after its underwhelming reviews and viewership so far. The show is only three episodes in, but I don’t see much buzz for it at all. It can’t make Peacock’s top ten and Television Stats reports a very low amount of online engagement about it.

It also airs on Friday nights, which has famously led to a bunch of cancellations for NBC, recently for shows like Stumble, Lopez vs. Lopez and Young Rock. It’s a shame that NBC’s only new comedy this season could be dead on arrival, especially considering all the great sitcoms the network has produced over the years. NBC’s other new show, Line of Fire, reportedly isn’t doing so hot either.

I’ll still be watching Newlyweds every week because I’m enjoying all its '90s nostalgia, and Curtis’s hilarious character, but I guess if it doesn't move forward I can't say I didn't see it coming. I don’t think it’s quite too late to make it a hit, so do me (and yourself) a favor and check it out!

#3713. Cities: Skylines 2 goes free-to-play, but only for a limited time

Cities: Skylines 2, Paradox Interactive’s ambitious follow-up to one of the best city builders of all time, has gone free-to-play. However, this will only apply for this weekend, with the event closing in the afternoon hours of Nov. 16.

The free-to-play model has more than doubled the game’s concurrent player count, bumping it from about 8,000 to over 16,000, according to SteamDB. People seem genuinely interested in checking the game out, though its less-than-stellar reviews and horrible reputation still seem to impact players’ willingness to actually spend any money on it, despite numerous discounts.

Speaking of which, Cities: Skylines 2 is also 30 percent off, or more if you go for the bundle and already own the original.

Ever since its original creators, Colossal Order, gave the game up to Paradox Interactive and Iceflake Studios, the game has gradually improved in overall quality. Things are undoubtedly moving at a snail’s pace, with Iceflake doing as much as it possibly can to salvage the title and reclaim some of that lost trust from the players. Despite their best efforts and, of course, several DLC releases, Cities: Skylines 2 still has a “mixed” rating on Steam, meaning it cannot be featured on the store’s front page or get any of that juicy free exposure from Valve.

The recent reviews fare much better, though. With 72 percent of those being positive, Cities 2 thus holds a “mostly positive” rating in this category, but players still have a lot of bones to pick with the game’s many systems, namely traffic and simulation, whereby bugs and issues that’ve been there from the start remain in the game.

I, for one, was extremely excited to get into Cities 2 ahead of its original release in 2023. The original Cities: Skylines is one of my favorite games of all time, and certainly my favorite city builder, and its sequel promised to up the ante on so many different levels. I was chiefly enamored by how detailed the new assets were in Cities 2, how big everything was, and how that would allow me to zoom in and see the minutiae from up close, but my hype evaporated once I got my hands on it.

The jank was unbearable, and the faulty simulation meant the game lied to you all the time, feeding you false information to make it seem like simulation was happening when, in fact, it was all fake.

Iceflake has since fixed many of these issues, and I will definitely be revisiting the game in the coming days.

#3711. Monster Hunter Wilds' upcoming Ascendance expansion may be getting a beta, some curious Steam backend updates suggest

Monster Hunter Wilds's first expansion, Ascendance, is set for release sometime next year. But, judging by some very suspect recent changes to the Wilds beta app on Steam, we may be playing some of the new stuff earlier than we thought.

On Steam, Capcom quietly updated the Monster Hunter Wilds Beta app to now say Monster Hunter Wilds: Ascendance Beta test. You can see the change log on SteamDB (via PC Gamer), which also shows an updated key art - all signs that point towards an impending beta for Ascendance.

The beta app is the same one those who played the original Wilds beta had in their library. Though the app was removed following the beta's conclusion, because the two share the same ID, the beta should be visible in users' list of played games under the new name. This could mean players won't need to sign up for the supposed Ascendance beta, seemingly only needing to download the new client.

Seeing as Ascendance itself doesn't have a release date, beyond a nebulous 2027 target, it's hard to speculate when Capcom plans to release the beta. Sometime early in 2027 would be a good guess, perhaps alongside a release date announcement.

Capcom has shown off Ascendance on multiple occasions, more recently in Sony's September State of Play, where we got to see a number of the expansion's new features. A few days later at Tokyo Game Show, we got a first look at returning Elder Dragon Teostra, which we can hunt in the expansion.

Capcom is keen for Ascendance to deliver the level of challenge Monster Hunter is known for, following feedback that the launch version of Wilds simply lacked that expected level of difficulty. While post-launch updates have certainly raised the level of challenge, Ascendance looks to be the next step up.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It’s a Small World is probably one of the most ridden attractions at Disneyland. It’s arguably the most famous, especially with the song that you’ll never escape once you get it in your head. Everyone can ride it, it gets you out of the heat during the hottest summer days, and it allows you to sit and relax for 15 minutes, which is longer than most other rides at the theme park. Because of all of that, I’ve always been surprised by how long the ride gets shut down for at Halloween in order to prepare for the holiday season.

As a result, I was pleasantly surprised to learn that the team responsible for transforming the attraction into It’s a Small World Holiday as a centerpiece for the Christmas season have been focused on reducing ride downtime. Sure, the overlay feels a bit chaotic, but it’s also a seasonal delight that will ensure you feel the holiday spirit. And according to the L.A. Times’ Mr. Todd’s Wild Ride newsletter, trimming the refurbishment time from 18 days down to 14 days will allow for approximately 74,000 more guests to be able to ride the attraction this year.

Christmas at theme parks is big business, so it makes sense that the Disneyland Resort would want to maximize what many consider to be the “most wonderful time of the year.” Disneyland during the holiday season is undeniably a magical place, with It’s a Small World Holiday being the centerpiece of that. While subtracting four days off the refurbishment time might not seem like a lot, any little bit helps.

It’s a Small World has been a popular attraction since it first debuted at the 1964 World’s Fair in New York, before opening first at Disneyland and then Magic Kingdom. If you’ve gotten to leisurely cruise down the water and take in all the sights in the Southern California theme park’s version of the ride, then you know how special and unique the façade is. Its transformation for the holidays is truly breathtaking, before you ever even see what the inside has to offer. And it sounds like a lot of this was made possible by doing something as simple as just storing the overlay pieces closer to where they actually need to be used.

While It’s a Small World is one of those rides that feels like it will always be a part of the Disneyland Resort no matter what changes get made around it, it hasn’t gone untouched over the years. Back in 2008, the attraction underwent a major refurbishment that included the addition of more than two dozen classic Disney characters to the ride, with the new dolls having been created in the original style of Mary Blair. And the 70th anniversary of the opening of Disneyland added the final verse to “It’s a Small World” that was penned by Richard Sherman before his death.

The best part of It’s a Small World Holiday has always been the brightly lit finale and its floor to ceiling decorations. Every doll in that room is embellished in some way, and its explosion of merriment is hard to ignore. I wouldn’t have been surprised if you told me that room alone took 18 days to deck out with Disney holiday magic. Still, I'm grateful that they have been able to shave a few days off of the refurbishment time because I’m glad to have the extra holiday merriment at the theme parks.

#3708. Viva Las Vegas, baby: Rainbow Six reportedly set to return to its high-rolling heights

Call up your buddies, set aside some cash, and get ready to leave it all at the craps tables: Rainbow Six is reportedly heading back to Vegas, baby, Vegas.

According to Insider Gaming’s Tom Henderson, three new projects are now in the works at Ubisoft Montreal, and one of them is a new release in the Rainbow Six: Vegas franchise, which last had an entry way back in 2008.

Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six: Vegas launched in 2006 on PC, PS3, Xbox 360, and even the PSP, and Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six: Vegas 2 followed two years later. Henderson says it’s currently unclear what the game will be, but sources state the new project codenamed “Spades” is “likely Vegas 3 rather than a remake, but only time will tell.” Even still, I think a remastered Vegas or Vegas 2 would be cause for excitement in some areas of the internet. He also said one of the other two games at Ubisoft Montreal is another title in the Rainbow universe, so Ubisoft seems to be doubling down and betting big on Rainbow.

The Vegas games followed the Rainbow team dispatched into Las Vegas, Nevada to battle terrorists, featuring a singleplayer campaign and competitive multiplayer that ended up on Major League Gaming’s Pro Circuit.

A return to the Vegas strip would likely be welcome news to many fans, as the Vegas games are regarded by many to be some of the best tactical FPS shooters from their era. I have a friend who I know will be particularly excited, as he was an avid Vegas player who tried to get me to join many times way back when.

#3707. World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunters have found the MMO's first hidden treasure

World of Warcraft secret hunters are a noble breed, known for scouring the MMO for years for hidden trinkets and treasures. With World of Warcraft: Forever's launch, they've uncovered a quest chain for an especially fancy sword.

Over the past week, members of the WoW Secret Hunters Discord found a quest chain that takes place entirely on the Zephras Isle, meaning you'll need to have access to the Skyborne elves to grab this sword. Navigating the island, you'll need to first pick up an ancient heirloom ring from the starting zone. Simple enough!

Then, you'll need to head to Duskwood to gather the Night Watchman's Torch, a handy light source primarily used to light up areas across the darkened woods near Stormwind. It turns out this torch has uses far beyond this one zone however, as taking it back to the Ruins of Ban'aethal on the Zephras Isle will reward you with a secret quest and the Ancient Hilt.

With the hilt and ring, you then must track down an Ancient Blade from one of several spawn locations on the Zephras Isle. Once you finally track it down, that's the end of part one of this quest chain. You get the sword: Eluvi'ana, which on its own isn't particularly strong, but is speculated to be upgraded later down the line.

You then need to get a corrupted water globe from either Darkshore or the Blackfathom Deeps dungeon depending on your faction, do a fetch quest for a hidden spirit in Ashenvale, then take your hoard of special quest items to a NPC in the new Shen'Dralar zone.

He won't give you the finished sword. Instead he sends you to gather more items from higher-level zones. You'll need to raid a secluded vault in Feralas that you can only see with the Ancient Hilt, dive underwater in Azshara, and kill Highborne Shades in Winterspring. Once you've done all that, you can then cleanse the orb up in Hyjal, speak to the fella back in Shen'Dralar, then shimmy over to the end game Dire Maul dungeon to speak to Prince Tortheldrin about *another* sword.

This is how far the World of Warcraft: Forever secret hunter community has gotten to. It's believed that grinding up the Shen'dralar reputation to Honoured is required for the next step, as Prince Tortheldrin pretty much says as much in his dialogue. So the hunt is still on!

These sorts of secrets make up an important part of any good MMO: the solving of mysteries in these vast digital open worlds. In retail WoW, I have fond memories of the Waist of Time quest chain, which was an arduous and comical grind for a fancy belt during the Battle for Azeroth expansion. This secret sword quest chain may very well evolve into something as legendary as that, at least I hope so!

#3705. As of this week, PlayStation 5 has surpassed 100 million consoles sold

PlayStation 5 has officially surpassed 100m consoles sold, Sony's updated sales data revealed. The milestone was reached on 10th November, almost exactly six years on from the console's launch.

The figure represents 'sell-in' units, meaning those shipped to retailers, as opposed to 'sell-through' which tracks consoles actually sold to consumers. In other words, the number of PS5s in people's homes is smaller than that 100m.

Nevertheless, this is an impressive achievement, and gets the PS5 ever closer to the PS4's 117m, which it achieved by June 2022. It also means the PS5 has almost matched the original PlayStation in units sold (102.4m). As impressive as the numbers are, historical data shows that PS5 sales have been in decline.

Sony hasn't shied away from discussing that fact in its earnings reports. 2.6m PS5 consoles were sold during the most recent quarter (Q2 of FY2026), well below the 4m sold over the same period the year prior. In fact, Q2 of FY2026 is the lowest second quarter on record in terms of units sold since the PS5's launch.

However, it's also worth noting that, small though it may be, the second quarter's result is higher than the first quarter's 1.6m, the second-lowest of any single quarter since the PS5's launch, beaten only by Q4 of FY2025's 1.5m.

If numbers don't recover in the third and fourth quarters, this may be the PS5's lowest year ever in terms of units sold. Although the second quarter's sales boost can be attributed to the high anticipation of Grand Theft Auto 6, the overall downturn is largely due to the console's higher price; Sony raised the PS5 and PS5 Pro's prices on several occasions since 2020. The company's bottom line, however, hasn't been affected much, as its plan to generate more revenue from its already-engaged audience continues to work.

#3704. "I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released" - former Tekken director Katsuhiro Harada trashes Microsoft's console in front of senior Xbox staff

Katsuhiro Harada, formerly director on the Tekken series, is known for not pulling his punches. This truth was reinforced recently, as he said he wished the Xbox Series S "wouldn't be released" at a developer panel. All while a member of the Xbox team was in the room.

Per Inven Global, Harada was sitting on a panel at the Console Game Developers Conference 2026 in South Korea. The panel was moderated by former Sony president Shuhei Yoshida, and featured Shift Up CTO DongKi Lee (Stellar Blade), Too Kyo Games CEO Kazutaka Kodaka (Dangenrompa), CD Projekt Red associate game director Paweł Sasko (Cyberpunk 2077), Ludeon Studios CEO Tynan Sylvester (Rimworld), and of course CEO of the newly formed VS Studio Katsuhiro Harada (Tekken).

The panel were asked about the advantages of console development, as well as specific challenges when creating games for certain platforms. Harada led the charge, speaking to the advantages consoles provide for fighting game developers, as the hardware is ideal for tournaments and esports events. Following this, he took an opportunity to speak about a console that drew his ire.

"That said, there's something I really want to say while I have the floor. Since a senior Xbox official is actually in attendance here today, I wish hardware like the Xbox Series S wouldn't be released," Harada said (translations to English via Inven Global). Harada then asked Sasko from the CD Projekt Red team whether he was "upset inside" because of the Xbox Series S.

Sasko proceeded to "burst out laughing" according to Inven Global, before responding: "It constantly throws challenges at us and forces us to optimize our code very cleanly."

Harada followed up with additional thoughts: "You just used a very polite and elegant way to say "Xbox Series S sucks," right? (laughs) Low memory is an issue, but the hardest part is that it's a device so similar to Series X while having awkwardly lower performance. When porting to Switch 2, developers can shift their mindset to 'Switch 2 is a distinct device for Nintendo fans!' But with Xbox, after delivering your absolute best output, it feels like having to do extra work for a slightly weaker child.

"Furthermore, in markets like the US, there are more Series S users than Series X users, so we can't just cut corners. Yet after launch, Series S users direct their complaints at us developers rather than Microsoft, asking 'Why is texture resolution lower only on Series S?'"

Sasko stepped up to offer some perks to the Series S. While he agreed that many players the full technical context behind the Series S' weaknesses, he pointed out that optimisation for weaker hardware like the Series S made games run "significantly better" across all platforms. He even had a Cyberpunk 2077 example, as optimisation work done for the Switch 2 version were applied to all platforms "to great effect". Sasko also pointed to the affordability side of the argument, saying that the cheaper price of the Series S allows for market expansion.

Harada responded: "Director Paweł packaged Series S so gracefully that the Microsoft representative in the audience keeps nodding along. I'm worried they'll feel reassured and release a successor like 'Helix S' for the next-gen Xbox as well (laughs)."

Here, Shift Up's DongKi Lee ended the topic with some optimism for Microsoft's future consoles: "Personally, I am looking forward to the next-gen Xbox 'Helix'. From an engineer's standpoint, if you provide us with a dev kit first in Korea as early as possible, we will put in our best efforts to develop for it."

Earlier this year Harada founded Vs Studio with SNK's support, with other veterans from Bandai Namco's Tekken team hopping on board for whatever it's working on. As for the Xbox Helix consoles, in this current hardware environment with bloated costs for RAM and other components, it's reportedly looking a tad expensive. Maybe a Series S equivalent is on the cards?

#3703. Layoffs, generative AI, and overtime: New study paints bleak picture of 2026 gaming industry

There’s a lot to be excited about in the gaming industry, as new awesome games are constantly being released. But the sad reality is that game development and the industry in general are in a very tough spot.

A new report, GDC’s State of the Game Industry: November 2026, illustrates this unfortunate sentiment and is quite depressing to read through. The top two topics in it are industry layoffs and generative AI, and yeah, that sounds about right when it comes to everybody’s mood inside game dev these days.

Citing people who work in the games industry surveyed from across the world (but mostly the US), GDC also pulled from a pool of 900 laid-off game workers to “dive deeper into their lived experiences.” And here’s the experience: a whopping 68 percent of those laid off from AAA studios were affected in the past year, while 27 percent of them have sent 100 or more job applications since being let go, and 54 percent of them are still unemployed.

And when it comes to sentiment within studios, things are looking and feeling bleak as a result of everything that’s been happening over the past few years, as evidenced by this chart:

A lot of that may have to do with AI usage in the industry, how much it’s being used, and how it’s threatening to take jobs. There’s no good answer for AI in game dev, but most surveyed agree that it should stay in non-creative use only.

But in general, 40 percent of those surveyed say that they use generative AI tools as part of their job, up from 36 percent last year, and 55 percent say that it’s having a negative impact on the industry.

The survey states that “55 percent of game industry professionals think generative AI is having a negative impact on the game industry, unchanged from last year’s 54 percent” and “workers in quality assurance and community support (76 percent) held the most unfavorable views, followed by game design (65 percent), visual and technical arts (65 percent), and audio (57 percent).” Meanwhile, 35% said, “generative AI is having a mixed impact on the game industry, while eight percent said it’s having a positive impact.”

And even with AI, work hours are getting hectic for many: 53 percent said they work over 40 hours weekly, with 13 percent saying they work 51 hours or more, on average, per week.

If you’d like to read the full report, check out the GDC website for all the detailed info.

Love Is Blind once again proves that love is not blind, or maybe shouldn’t be, with another disastrous season. However, this may be one of the show’s most unsuccessful seasons in terms of marriages and long-term relationships. The one marriage from the season didn’t even last a year.

An interesting reunion can usually redeem a less-than-exciting season of Love is Blind, which you can watch with a Netflix subscription. We have seen many do just that. However, this reunion confirmed just how disappointing Season 11 is. It magnified Love is Blind’s issues.

Warning: Love is Blind Season 11 reunion spoilers are ahead. Proceed with caution.

I have watched all 11 seasons of Love Is Blind, and the reunions are getting worse. These are supposed to be an opportunity to dig into some of the biggest unanswered questions. They could be a chance to hold people accountable for questionable behavior from previous episodes.

Hosts Nick and Vanessa Lachey achieve some of these things, but not fully. Rob Feeley had one of the season’s biggest moments. It led to many online discussions about his and his friends’ problematic behavior. The reunion barely addresses it.

Other things aren’t fully addressed, including details of some of the breakups. For example, we’re left confused about Michaella Giorgio and Matt Waldrip’s failed relationship. We leave the season with a lot more questions than answers.

The whole point of the reunion is to get answers and closure for the viewers. Even the messiest seasons usually have some bright spots, but Love Is Blind: Boston doesn’t seem to have any. This makes us worry even more about the series’ future.

The reunion had bromance montages, an engagement announcement from someone who was barely on the season, a focus on some men who were barely on the show, a look at Blake Carver’s life in the sea, and a musical number. It seemed like the Love Is Blind Season 11 reunion wanted to do everything but focus on what viewers care about: information about the couples.

I know the show wanted to balance some lighthearted moments with the drama and heaviness. However, they just felt out of place. It took away from the really interesting parts of the reunion. Additionally, it felt extremely ironic that a show that’s supposed to focus on proving love can work under extreme circumstances chose to have “Stop the Wedding!” by Ashe as the season’s theme song.

It further emphasizes how much Love Is Blind doesn’t take itself seriously anymore. We don’t know if the producers still care at all about having successful couples.

Automatically, the Love Is Blind reunion felt uncomfortable. It just became increasingly that way as it progressed. It was an intense season, but the producers could have done more to make the tension less intense. It was either too intense or ridiculous with showing unnecessary things like montages.

Love Is Blind has had plenty of iconic moments, so the show has the capability for that. However, it’s losing its way in producing a well-executed, compelling show about relationships. The season as a whole and the reunion highlights this problem. Hopefully, they can start to pull it back to its old glory in the upcoming season.

We still think Love Is Blind, but it could use some help.

The extraction shooter-slasher game enters early access on Steam on 3rd December, and there's good news if you're eager to try it out before then.

The game's alternate history, plague-ravaged European setting gives it a grimey, steel-and-mud look few games have.

Beyond the in-match experience, Good Fun's ambitions extend to Hunger's MMO-style progression, its hub area with distinct characters and varied playable classes - all of which can be sampled in the upcoming beta.

Hunger just came off a very successful closed beta, which clearly didn't suffer by kicking off right alongside Modern Warfare 4's DMZ early access. Hunger is currently among Steam's most-wishlisted games, with over 700,000 wishlists, according to the developer.

Having trouble making a Horde character in PvP lately? You're not alone.

If you’ve been eager to hop into World of Warcraft: Forever, create a Horde character, say “lok’tar ogar!” (victory or death!) after an intense PvP match, you’re going to have to wait. There’s an ongoing faction lock on Horde characters in PvP rulesets until further notice.

In a game like WoW, premised on being big on faction warfare, achieving some form of balance across player numbers ensures no one side dominates PvP. And since Forever does have a dedicated mega-realm (ruleset) for PvP players, this faction lock has become a source of frustration.

We’ll look into what we know so far, and update you once it’s finally been lifted.

The faction lock happens when you try to switch over to the PvP ruleset and create a Horde character. Chances are, you’ll be stopped by the game. The error box will state this is due to a “population imbalance.”

If you’ve ever encountered faction restrictions in WoW before, this is a similar situation. Just like the error says, it’s very likely that one faction probably had a lot more players than the other.

“While even the most extreme case in a region is currently at roughly a 55/45 split, that is not as close as we want it to be,” community manager Kaivax said in a post. “Our goal is to bring things as close to a 50/50 faction balance as possible.”

There is no definitive fix for the faction lock as of writing. Some common (albeit unproven) solutions include the following:

There has been no proof that paying for a new account or getting an account boost can fix the lock, so better to stay safe and avoid these. If you want to wait a couple of minutes, avoid using an auto-clicker to be on the safe side.

While waiting, you could also do the following:

Perhaps the most common “answer” to the lock problem is to create a character in the other faction to help balance the population. Unfortunately, this will lock your account’s PvP ruleset to that faction.

If you already have a character in the PvE ruleset, you can hop on there and enjoy its more casual leveling experience. You can still toggle World PvP via the options menu.

Should you want to take the game’s adventuring fantasy more seriously, maybe the RP-PvP ruleset works for you. This just has the added requirement of actually roleplaying your character, so speaking in dialogue, following cues for anything out-of-character, and just fully immersing in Azeroth. Perfect if you want to roleplay your character’s heritage on top of high-stakes PvP.

Character creation restrictions in PvP rulesets weren’t just exclusive to the Horde, however. Blizzard also locked the creation of Alliance characters to some degree, in a bid to ensure character populations across each faction are as balanced as realistically possible.

As such, you might have some difficulty creating characters of a specific faction in a specific region:

Kaivax assured this is temporary and helps the “long-term health of the ruleset,” especially now when guilds are slowly being established.

Other players took to other avenues to explore the faction lock situation as well. While there’s no definite solution aside from waiting, here are other things you should take into account:

There are also other players who have already experienced some version of faction locking before it got widespread. They also posted about it in the Blizzard forums.

However, Yryadorne from customer service clarified that their team isn’t able to unlock this manually.

Some players asked whether trial accounts also affected the count. These are accounts where you could only play for free until Level 20 (with restrictions) without a subscription. Kaivax replied that their testing concluded the trial accounts had nothing to do with the imbalance. They explained that the 55/45 split focused on the “active logged-in population” of players across all levels.

There’s no evidence that creating a lot of trial accounts would fix the faction balance, especially if part of the consideration is that they are “actively” logged in.

Just to be on the safe side, it might be a good idea to check if your Horde lock is related ot any other character creation errors. Blizzard outlined this list, which could be a useful reference:

A lot of players expressed frustration with the inability to create characters in their favored Faction, especially those who want to sink their teeth into PvP in Forever.

The situation has been particularly difficult for players who also want to play with friends of one faction, only to find out it’s currently locked.

One Blizzard forum post even requested some form of compensation, as there’s no proper communication surrounding the faction lock. Other threads also called out the lack of any virtual queue, estimated waiting time, or any way of knowing how long until the restriction is lifted.

The idea of faction-locking isn’t new to Forever, but it certainly came as a shocker to players still getting used to the idea of having one mega-realm to play on.

Things were different in the OG release and Classic, where you could have characters in different realms. Back then, you could only be Horde on one PvP realm and Alliance on another. Faction rules only applied to new players when one faction was starting to crowd a specific realm, so newcomers had to adjust by joining the rival group.
